 AN CHÚIRT UACHTARACH 

 THE SUPREME COURT 

 S:AP:IE:2024:000124 

 [2026] IESC 2 

 Between/ 

 G.M. 

 Applicant/Appellant 

 AND 

   

 I.M. 

 Respondent 

 AND 

 THE ATTORNEY GENERAL 

 Notice Party 

 Judgment of Ms. Justice Dunne  delivered on the 23 January 2026 

 Introduction 

 1.                      This appeal concerns the nature, scope and parameters of the courts' jurisdiction to impose constraints on the entitlement of a serial or vexatious litigant to institute legal proceedings. In particular, this appeal raises the question of the courts' entitlement to make an Isaac Wunder order in family law proceedings concerning child access and/or maintenance disputes, and the circumstances in which such an order can be made. 

 2.                      It is well established that where a court is satisfied that a litigant has persistently instituted vexatious or frivolous proceedings, it may make an order in the exercise of its inherent powers restraining that person from instituting any further proceedings without first obtaining the leave of the court. Such an order, commonly referred to as an Isaac Wunder order, derives its name from the decision of this Court in Wunder v. Irish Hospitals Trust (1940) Ltd (Unreported, Supreme Court, 15 January 1968). The decision in Riordan v. An Taoiseach (No 4) [2001] IESC 83 , [2001] 3 IR 365 affirmed the broad and inherent jurisdiction of the courts to make such orders where necessary to protect parties " from unnecessary harassment and expenses " and prevent abuses of court processes (at p. 370).  

 3.                      However, the question of a court's entitlement to make an Isaac Wunder order in family law proceedings pertaining to child access and/or maintenance disputes has never been comprehensively addressed by this Court, and raises a distinct set of considerations which do not typically arise in other civil law proceedings, including but not limited to: the constitutional obligation on the courts to consider the " best interests " of the child under Article 42A of the Constitution, the affected parent's right of access to the court under Article 40.3, and a consideration of the rights guaranteed by the European Convention on Human Rights ("the Convention"), including the right to a fair trial under Article 6 and the right to respect for private and family life under Article 8. Further, an issue arises as to the jurisdiction of courts of local and limited jurisdiction to make such powers and the extent of any limitation on the exercise of such jurisdiction. 

 Background 

 4.                      This appeal arises out of protracted family law proceedings between the appellant and the respondent, in circumstances where the parties were formerly in an intimate relationship and have a minor child together. The parties are now estranged and have been engaged in proceedings pertaining to the access and maintenance of their child since 2012. On 8 th December, 2015, the District Court issued an order varying a previous order for access dated 30 th July, 2015. The respondent appealed this to the Circuit Court, which, after more than forty court listings, made a final determination on the issues of both access and maintenance on 23 rd May, 2022. The Circuit Court's ruling included specific access arrangements for the child and an order for the appellant to pay outstanding maintenance arrears to the respondent, as well as discharging the existing maintenance order and directing the appellant to make ad hoc contributions towards any future child rearing expenses incurred by the respondent. 

 5.                      The Court further ordered the appellant to pay 50 per cent of the total legal costs incurred by the respondent in the family law proceedings, attributing increased costs to the appellant's unmeritorious conduct, including his persistent breaches of the access order and repeated applications to the Court. During submissions on costs, counsel for the appellant stated that the issue of repeated litigation could be dealt with by way of an Isaac Wunder order, instead of a costs order. The Circuit Court judge accepted this submission and made an order, of her own motion, restricting the appellant from taking any further proceedings against the respondent in the District Court, the Circuit Court or in any other court without first obtaining leave of the Circuit Court. 

 6.                      On 19 th August, 2022, the appellant made an ex parte application for leave to apply for judicial review to the High Court. At paragraph (d)(ii) of the appellant's statement of grounds, the following relief was sought: 

 " An Order of Certiorari pursuant to Order 84 rule 18 of the Rules of the Superior Courts, by way of application for Judicial Review, quashing the Order of the Respondent dated the 23 rd May 2022. " 

 7.                      The appellant also sought inter alia a declaration that the Circuit Court had acted in breach of its duties by relying on evidence which was not properly before it, and by not permitting the appellant to give or produce evidence in the course of the hearing. The appellant averred in his verifying affidavit that the Circuit Court admitted into evidence material that was neither provided on affidavit nor adduced in the course of oral testimony and did not permit cross-examination of the respondent , thereby denying him his due process rights in accordance with the Rules of Court and the Constitution. This application was granted by Simons J. on 19 th August, 2022. In response, the respondent issued a motion on 19 th October, 2022 to set aside the grant of leave, contending that these proceedings were grounded upon an affidavit that was manifestly and factually incorrect, and further, were pursued in breach of the Isaac Wunder order granted by the Circuit Court. 

 High Court Judgment ( [2023] IEHC 95 ) 

 8.                      In a judgment dated 6 th March, 2023, Simons J. addressed the matter of the Isaac Wunder order purportedly imposed by the Circuit Court. Setting aside the question of the Circuit Court's jurisdiction to make a restraining order, Simons J. held that while the High Court has an inherent jurisdiction to restrain the taking of proceedings in the lower courts, the Circuit Court could not frustrate the exercise of the High Court's supervisory jurisdiction by obliging a party to obtain from it prior permission before instituting judicial review proceedings. If and insofar as the order of 23 rd May, 2022 purported to " oust the High Court's full original jurisdiction ", Simons J. found this to represent an error on the face of the record (judgment, para. 16). 

 9.                      Turning to the merits of the respondent's application, Simons J. held that this was an appropriate case in which to set aside the grant of leave, in circumstances where there had been material non-disclosure on the part of the appellant ( Adams v. Director of Public Prosecutions [2001] IESC 27 , [2001] 2 ILRM 401 ; Ryan v. Governor v. Mountjoy Prison [2020] IESC 8 , [2021] I.R. 590). In particular, he determined the appellant's characterisation of the Circuit Court hearing of 23 rd May 2022 as per his statement of grounds and verifying affidavit to be grossly misleading and failed to disclose the protracted litigation history between the parties. Simons J. concluded that the appellant's contention that the Circuit Court hearing had been conducted in breach of fair procedures was untenable; accordingly, the grant of leave was set aside. 

 Court of Appeal Judgments ( [2024] IECA 45 and [2024] IECA 169 ) 

 10.                  The appellant sought to appeal the decision of the High Court on the grounds that the trial judge's finding of material non-disclosure was incorrect, and further, pertained only to those stateable grounds for judicial review concerning the outstanding maintenance order and order for costs imposed by the Circuit Court. It was contended that the appellant had clearly applied for leave to review the entirety of the orders made by the Circuit Court on 23 rd May, 2022 as per para. (d)(ii) of his original statement of grounds, including the Isaac Wunder order, notwithstanding that there was no direct challenge to the making of that order in the appellant's pleadings. 

 11.                  In a judgment dated 28 th February, 2024 ( [2024] IECA 45 ), the Court of Appeal ( Woulfe, Ní Raifeartaigh, Power JJ.) upheld the High Court's finding that the previous grant of leave should be set aside on the grounds that there had been material misstatements of fact and/or material non-disclosure on the part of the appellant. This finding was, however, subject to the qualification that the non-disclosure was not material to the appellant's challenge to the Isaac Wunder order, with Woulfe J. finding the High Court's original grant of leave to be sufficiently capacious to encompass the seeking of an order of certiorari to quash that order, as set out at para. (d)(ii) of the appellant's statement of grounds. There was therefore a surviving basis for the appellant's judicial review challenge and the order of the High Court was varied on this ground. 

 12.                  The Court directed a supplemental hearing to determine the nature of the consequential orders arising from this decision and whether the proceedings ought to be remitted to the High Court for determination. In a second judgment dated 28 th June, 2024 ( [2024] IECA 169 ), the Court of Appeal ( Woulfe, Ní Raifeartaigh, Power JJ.) noted that the parties had agreed that the Court would make an order quashing the Isaac Wunder order of the Circuit Court and proceed to entertain a new application by the respondent for a fresh order. Delivering the judgment, Woulfe J. emphasised the broad nature of the Court's jurisdiction to grant an Isaac Wunder order, as recognised by this Court in Riordan (No. 4) . He endorsed the specific factors set out by Irvine J. to which a court may have regard when making such an order, as stated at para. 73 of her judgment in Burke v. Judge Fulham [2010] IEHC 448 : 

 " Amongst the factors a court may consider justify the making of such an order are first, the bringing of one or more actions to determine an issue already determined by another court of competent jurisdiction; second, where it is obvious that an action cannot succeed or would lead to no possible good; third, actions brought for an improper purpose including harassment and oppression of other parties; fourth, the rolling forward of issues into subsequent actions ; fifth, the whole history of the matter, sixth; a failure on the part of a party instituting proceedings to pay the costs of previous proceedings wherein they were unsuccessful; and finally the conduct of a party who persistently pursues unsuccessful appeals. " 

 13.                  Applying the Burke principles to the present case, Woulfe J. first assessed whether the appellant had brought one or more actions to determine an issue already determined by another court. Addressing the appellant's contention that all appearance dates subsequent to the District Court order of 18 th December, 2015 were brought about as a consequence of the respondent's appeal to the Circuit Court, rather than any action instituted by him, Woulfe J. agreed with the approach of Butler J. in Scanlan v. Gilligan [2021] IEHC 825 that an Isaac Wunder order could be granted against a person who has not previously instituted proceedings, but becomes the de facto moving party in the unnecessary extension or prolongation of litigation as a result of their conduct. Woulfe J. referred in particular to the unsuccessful judicial review proceedings instituted by the appellant in 2018 to challenge an interim access order of the Circuit Court dated 27 th June, 2018, in circumstances where he had failed to comply with any aspect of that order, in addition to his constant applications and attendances before the Circuit Court since the District Court access order of December 2015. 

 14.                  With regard to the second Burke factor, Woulfe J. was satisfied that the present proceedings constituted an action which " could not succeed and would lead to no possible good ", for the reasons set out in the Court's principal judgment. Thirdly, he found that while the appellant's purpose in bringing previous applications was to achieve access or greater access to his son, this purpose also included the harassment and oppression of the respondent, including multiple unfounded complaints against her and aggressive behaviour which resulted in her being required to obtain a safety order from the District Court. Turning to the fourth Burke factor of the " rolling forward of issues into subsequent actions ", Woulfe J. referred to the appellant's pattern of seeking to employ High Court judicial review proceedings to frustrate the outcome of proceedings decided against him in the Circuit Court. Fifth, the Court had regard to the whole history of these proceedings, including the consistent pattern of unmeritorious conduct on the part of the appellant and the High Court finding of material non-disclosure. Sixth, Woulfe J. found that the appellant had failed to pay the respondent the costs of previous proceedings wherein he was unsuccessful. Finally, the Court considered that the present judicial review proceedings involved the pursuit of an almost entirely unsuccessful appeal by the appellant. 

 15.                  On account of these factors, the Court of Appeal concluded that permitting the appellant to continue to litigate against the respondent " would be unfair and oppressive ... and a waste of scarce court time and resources to the detriment of other litigants " (judgment, para. 30). The Court determined that this order ought to restrain the appellant from instituting any proceedings against the respondent including appeal proceedings, whether in the District Court, Circuit Court, High Court or Court of Appeal, except with prior leave of the President of that Court or a judge nominated by the President. 

 Determination 

 16.                  The appellant was granted leave to appeal to this Court on 14 th October, 2024 ([2024] IESCDET 117). The Court determined this case to raise issues of general public importance as to the circumstances in which an Isaac Wunder order can be made in respect of applications for access and maintenance. The Attorney General was invited to join as a notice party to these proceedings in circumstances where this appeal concerns a matter of broad application in the area of family law and court procedure. 

 17.                  The Court granted leave on the following four issues: 

 (1)    Is a court dealing with applications for access and/or maintenance in respect of a child entitled to make an Isaac Wunder order against a party to those proceedings? 

 And, if so entitled, 

 (2)    The basis on which such an order may be made. 

 And further, if so entitled, 

 (3)    Whether there was any error by the Court of Appeal in making the Isaac Wunder order in these proceedings? 

 And further, 

 (4)    What powers may a court generally exercise when presented with a serial litigant or someone who prolongs or disrupts proceedings on a repeated basis including disrupting or prolonging proceedings by misrepresenting what occurred in court on a previous occasion? 

 Submissions 

 Issues 1 and 2: Jurisdiction of the Courts to Make an Isaac Wunder Order in Family Law Proceedings Concerning Child Access and Maintenance Disputes 

 18.                  The appellant submits that while the courts enjoy an inherent jurisdiction to prevent abuse of process and vexatious litigation in civil proceedings, the application of an Isaac Wunder order in family law proceedings concerning access and/or maintenance issues fundamentally disregards the nature of these disputes. The appellant emphasises the requirement for ongoing court intervention in the family law context and the constitutional obligation to consider the best interests of the child under Article 42A.4. Should this Court find the making of Isaac Wunder orders appropriate and just in access and maintenance proceedings, the appellant submits that such an order should be subject to strict safeguards regarding the welfare of the child, the affected party's constitutional rights, including their right of access to the court under Article 40.3, and the affected party's rights guaranteed by the Convention, including the right to a fair trial under Article 6 and the right to respect for private and family life under Article 8. 

 19.                  To this end, the appellant relies on jurisprudence of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) concerning the interaction between Articles 6 and 8 and domestic restrictions placed on parental rights of access ( A.D. and O.D. v. the United Kingdom ( App. No. 28680/06, 16 th June, 2010 ); T.P. and K.M. v. the United Kingdom (App. No. 28945/95, 10 th May, 2001)). In Elsholz v. Germany (App. No. 25735/94, 13 th July, 2000) for example, the Grand Chamber held that while domestic authorities may enjoy a wide margin of appreciation when assessing the necessity of taking a child into care, " a stricter scrutiny is called for in respect of any further limitations " such as restrictions placed on parental rights of access, and of any legal safeguards designed to secure an effective protection of the right of parents and children to respect for their family life (para. 49). Further, the appellant contends that the Isaac Wunder order's preliminary leave requirement involves further time, expense and delay in respect of access to the child, thereby depriving the affected parent of his or her right to a timely hearing, as guaranteed by Article 6 of the Convention and the procedural requirements implicit in Article 8 ( Paparrigopoulos v. Greece (App. No. 61657/16, 30 th June, 2022 , para. 49)), or otherwise exposing the parent to loss of contact with the child due to the passage of time ( Fernández Cabanillas v. Spain (App. No. 22731/11, 18 th February, 2014, para. 48). 

 20.                  The appellant compares the imposition of Isaac Wunder orders in Ireland with the approach of other common law jurisdictions to vexatious litigation to underscore what he contends are deficiencies with the Irish system. He submits that the Irish approach lacks the flexibility, proportionality, legal certainty, and structured oversight found in the statutory regimes of the UK, Canada, and Australia governing vexatious litigation. In particular, the appellant commends the 'graduated' or 'tiered' model of civil restraint orders of the UK introduced by Rule 3.11 of the Civil Procedure Rules 1998, and the Family Procedure Rules 2010 in the context of family law proceedings. The UK regime provides for three different types of civil restraint orders which are progressively more restrictive, with defined temporal limits that are tailored to the litigant's behaviour and litigation history. By contrast, the appellant submits that the Isaac Wunder order is unduly broad in scope (applying to all future proceedings irrespective of the nature of the claim), indefinite in duration, made on an ad hoc basis in the absence of statutory guidance, and lacking formal mechanisms for appeal or review. Ultimately, it is contended that the broad discretion conferred on the courts in this jurisdiction may result in the imposition of civil restraining orders that are disproportionate and excessively restrictive, thereby violating the principles of natural justice and constitutional rights. 

 21.                  The respondent submits that a court is entitled to make an Isaac Wunder order in the exercise of its inherent jurisdiction in circumstances where a custodial parent is compelled to engage in protracted litigation, particularly in light of the liberal right of access to the courts which the Guardianship of Infants Act 1964 affords non-custodial parents, and the wide availability of civil legal aid in family law proceedings. It is submitted that neither the appellant's constitutional right of access to the courts nor his Convention right to a fair hearing are directly interfered with by the making of an Isaac Wunder order; rather, as stated by Noonan J. in Leslie Fitzsimons v. Bank of Scotland [2019] IECA 336 , the order operates as a " proportionate filtering mechanism to protect the opposing party from the injustice of having to incur what are often very significant and unrecoverable costs " (para. 24). 

 22.                  The respondent notes that the ECtHR has, similarly, found certain judicial measures designed to prevent abuse of the civil process to comply with the right of access to the courts. To this end, the respondent relies on Tolstoy Miloslavsky v. the United Kingdom (App. No.18139/91) (1995) 20 EHRR 442 in which the Court affirmed the inherent jurisdiction of a domestic court to control its own processes in the context of a dismissal of the applicant's appeal due to his failure to provide security for costs previously ordered. The respondent further distinguishes Elsholz and TP , which are relied on by the appellant, on the basis that those cases did not concern the fairness or proportionality of imposing a civil restraining order in family law proceedings, but the question of whether the domestic courts had violated the applicants' right to family life under Article 8 for reasons of procedural unfairness inherent in the proceedings. In the present case, the respondent notes that the appellant does not take issue with the procedural fairness of these proceedings; indeed, he consented to a determination of a fresh Isaac Wunder order. In respect of procedural safeguards, the respondent highlights the obligation of the President or nominated judge to determine an application for leave in conformity with the Constitution and the Convention where an Isaac Wunder order is granted, and the capacity of an affected parent to apply at any stage for the requisite leave to bring further proceedings against the other parent thereafter. 

 23.                  Should this Court determine that the making of an Isaac Wunder order constitutes an interference with Article 8 of the Convention, the respondent submits that such an interference is proportionate and necessary when made pursuant to governing Irish jurisprudence, being a measure which pursues a " legitimate " aim under Article 8(2) and can be regarded as " necessary in a democratic society ". The respondent rejects the appellant's contention that the preliminary leave requirement infringes his right to a timely hearing or exposes him to loss of contact with his child, noting that an Isaac Wunder order is only obtained in exceptional cases upon proof of unjustified or oppressive prolongation of proceedings. Where further proceedings are necessary to protect the affected parent's rights, leave can expect to be granted, and proceedings are capable of being issued, within a short period of time thereafter. 

 24.                  With regard to the legal framework of England and Wales, the respondent notes that the superior courts have affirmed their inherent jurisdiction, as distinct from statutory rules, to protect their own processes from abuse by issuing civil restraint orders ( Bhamjee v Forsdick (No. 2) [2004] 1 WLR 88 ). While it is acknowledged that civil restraint orders are not commonly made in the context of child proceedings given the availability of a parallel statutory mechanism restricting litigation in s. 91(14) of the Children Act 1989, the respondent notes that it is permissible for the courts to make such orders of their own motion in exceptional cases, citing A.E.Y. v. A.L. [2018] EWHC 3253 (Fam) , in which Knowles J. characterised such orders as a " useful means of protecting the family justice system from abuse " (para. 68). Finally, while the respondent accepts that Article 42A of the Constitution requires the child's best interests to be the " paramount consideration " in any proceedings concerning adoption, guardianship or custody, it is submitted that the appellant's submissions on this point centre on the effect of the alleged curtailment on his right of access to the courts only. Insofar as the child's best interests are concerned, it is submitted that unjustly prolonged litigation may cause avoidable distress and threaten to deplete the finances of the custodial parent, on whom the child in question is dependent for stability and financial support. 

 Issue 3: The Court of Appeal Order 

 25.                  The appellant contends that the Court of Appeal erred by making an Isaac Wunder order without proper consideration of less intrusive measures that would achieve the same objective, while respecting his fundamental rights and the best interests of the child under Article 42A of the Constitution. The appellant submits that the imposition of an indefinite and blanket Isaac Wunder order failed to strike the balance between protecting the respondent's rights and preserving the appellant's right to seek access to the court in access and maintenance proceedings concerning his child. He argues that a time-limited or specific issue-related order would be a more proportionate measure in the circumstances. 

 26.                  The appellant submits that the Court of Appeal erred in failing to provide adequate reasons as to why its order was necessary and proportionate, and not restricted to a " specified type of family law litigation " (judgment, para. 30). Further, it is contended that the order was imposed without specific findings that the appellant's previous applications were frivolous or without merit, as the Court of Appeal failed to adequately distinguish between genuine attempts to modify access or maintenance arrangements and vexatious litigation. In this respect, the appellant submits that the Court's finding that his judicial review proceedings would not succeed and " lead to no possible good " (judgment, para. 23) cannot be reconciled with its finding that the appellant's previous applications were brought for the " proper purpose of achieving access or greater access to his son " (judgment, para. 24). The appellant concludes that the Court of Appeal decision does not accord with the principles of legal certainty, proportionality and transparency, and has the potential to lead to injustice in future family law cases. 

 27.                  The respondent submits that the Court of Appeal did not err in applying an Isaac Wunder order without proper consideration of less intrusive measures. It is submitted that such an order was justified having regard to the exceptional circumstances of the present case, the order being the only appropriate remedy to protect the Court from abuse of its processes and the respondent and child from the negative effects of oppressive litigious conduct. With regard to the Court's finding that the appellant's action was one which would " lead to no possible good ", the respondent clarifies that Woulfe J.'s subsequent reference to applications that may or may not have been brought for proper purposes appears to have been a reference to historical access applications and not to the extant judicial review application. The respondent contends that had the Court refused to make an Isaac Wunder order by reason of the proceedings concerning child-related matters, the respondent would have been divested of a critical remedy. 

 Issue 4: General Powers of the Court when Presented with Serial Litigants 

 28.                  The appellant states that the Irish courts have traditionally relied on their inherent jurisdiction, rooted in the common law and judicial discretion, to manage abusive or vexatious litigants and safeguard the judicial process. He submits that any restriction on a litigant's access to the courts must adhere to the principles of proportionality and legal certainty, as protected under Irish law and the Convention ( Brumarescu v. Romania (App. No. 28342/95) (1999) VII E.H.R.R. 862). It is submitted that the mechanisms available to the Irish courts do not fully accord with these principles and restraining orders ought to be tailored to address the specific disruptive conduct of a litigant. The appellant once again advocates for the introduction of a calibrated and structured approach to civil restraining orders, as applied in the UK. 

 29.                  The respondent highlights a number of measures that a civil court may take when presented with a serial litigant. First, a court is empowered to strike out the proceedings under O. 19, r. 28 of the Rules of the Superior Courts (RSC) if the proceedings disclose no reasonable cause of action, or are frivolous or vexatious. A court can also dismiss proceedings if the litigant's actions unduly delay the case or are intended to obstruct justice. A court may exercise its inherent jurisdiction or statutory powers to impose cost orders and/or employ case management as a means to discourage delay, e.g. the option to impose strict timelines under the Courts and Civil Law (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2013. Further, where a misrepresentation of prior proceedings is at issue, a court may order a transcript of those proceedings to clarify matters. However, the respondent contends that these alternatives are incapable of addressing a serial family law litigant, due to the absence of bars to repeat litigation in child-related proceedings. Applicants to other civil proceedings are, by contrast, subject to the rules of res judicata, issue estoppel, and the 'one action rule' in Henderson v. Henderson (1843) 3 Hare 100 , 67 ER 313 . The respondent concludes that the absence of statutory rules in Ireland governing civil restraining orders only serves to reinforce the need to retain the Isaac Wunder order as a necessary judicial tool to protect the courts' civil processes and prevent abuse by misconducting litigants. 

 Attorney General Submissions 

 30.                  The submissions of the Attorney General focus on the broader issues of law arising from questions 1, 2 and 4 of this Court's determination granting leave. They concern the general nature, scope and parameters of the courts' jurisdiction to impose constraints on the entitlement of a party to initiate legal proceedings, and the specific application of this power to family law proceedings concerning access and/or maintenance disputes. 

 31.                  The Attorney General emphasises that the Isaac Wunder order is only one illustration of the long-established, inherent power of the courts to protect their processes from misuse and abuse; as Whelan J. explained in Kearney v. Bank of Scotland plc [2020] IECA 92 , it " form [s] part of the panoply of the courts' inherent powers to regulate their own process " (para. 132). It is submitted that Irish jurisprudence reveals two broad principles to underpin the use of this inherent power: (i) the protection of other parties from serial, abusive or vexatious litigation (a 'private interest') and (ii) the necessity to protect the court process itself against repeated or excessive misuse of court time and resources (a 'public interest'). The Attorney submits that the nature of the interest at issue will often determine the type of order imposed by a court; the protection of the private interest may, for example, be met by orders which limit the capacity of an individual to bring any further action against a specific party while the protection of the public interest may necessitate a broad, all-encompassing order. 

 32.                  It is noted that the courts of England and Wales have continued to develop the inherent power to protect their own processes, alongside the broad statutory power created by s. 42 of the Supreme Court Act 1981, which empowers a court to make an indefinite order constraining a vexatious litigant from initiating proceedings without leave of the High Court, on the application of the Attorney General. The Attorney General draws attention to the fact that this development has been expressly justified by a perceived need to protect the public rather than the private interest in preventing vexatious litigation. In Bhamjee (No 2) , for example, the Court of Appeal considered that the " totally unmeritorious waste of the resources of a court ", including the time and resources of court staff, lawyer or judges, was itself sufficient to justify the granting of injunctive relief. As noted by the appellant above, the parameters of the courts' powers have been somewhat formalised by the Civil Procedure Rules 1998 and the introduction of the limited, extended, and general civil restraining orders under Practice Direction 3C. 

 33.                  The Attorney General highlights a number of mechanisms to which the inherent power of the Irish courts could extend when presented with a serial litigant or someone who prolongs or disrupts proceedings on a repeated basis, including: the striking out of proceedings (O. 19, r. 28 of the RSC); the dismissal of proceedings where the litigant's conduct makes their continuation impossible ( Burke v. Adjudication Officer and Workplace Relations Commission [2023] IEHC 360 ); the making of an order restraining a litigant from bringing proceedings without permission against a named party or in particular proceedings ( O'Connor v. Property Registration Authority of Ireland [2019] IECA 235 ); the making of an order requiring a litigant to provide security for costs ( Ulster Bank DAC & Ors v. McDonagh & Ors (No. 3) [2024] IEHC 609 ); and the use of the contempt jurisdiction ( Walsh v. Minister for Justice [2020] 1 I.R. 488). 

 34.                  The Attorney General emphasises that the use of these powers ought to be balanced against competing considerations, including the constitutional right of access to the courts under Article 40.3 and the rights guaranteed by Article 6 of the Convention. However, it is submitted that this right may be subject to appropriate limitations, provided that the impugned measure satisfies the proportionality test articulated by the ECtHR in Tolstoy Miloslavsky (para. 59): 

 " [T]he Court must be satisfied, firstly, that the limitations applied do not restrict or reduce the access left to the individual in such a way or to such an extent that the very essence of the right is impaired. Secondly, a restriction must pursue a legitimate aim and there must be a reasonable relationship of proportionality between the means employed and the aim sought to be achieved ..." 

 35.                  It is submitted that the question of whether the making of a particular order is a proportionate means of protecting court processes against misuse is case-specific, but could involve the weighing of the factors identified by the Court of Appeal in Kearney v. Bank of Scotland plc [2020] IECA 92 (para. 132) in the context of applying an Isaac Wunder order. These principles include, but are not limited to: the history of litigation between the parties; whether there are good grounds for believing there will be further proceedings instituted by the litigant; the issue of costs and the litigant's history of discharging costs orders; the interests of the common good and the need to ensure that limited court resources are available to those who require them; the stigmatising effect of an Isaac Wunder order; and the availability of an order to strike out or dismiss the proceedings in the circumstances. 

 36.                  The Attorney General states that there is no reason in principle why orders restricting the entitlement of a party to initiate legal proceedings should not be available in family law proceedings. However, there are considerations which suggest they should be applied sparingly in this context, including the fact that family law proceedings may be the subject of ongoing court applications, that issues concerning the care and welfare of children may involve a less adversarial form of inquiry by the courts, and that these cases may engage additional constitutional considerations under Articles 41, 42 and 42A of the Constitution. In this respect, the Attorney General accepts that any constraint imposed on a parent's right to institute proceedings ought to be considered in a child-centred manner. 

 37.                  There is, nonetheless, domestic authority for the making of Isaac Wunder orders, or similar restraint orders, in the family law context. The threshold of exceptionality was considered to be met by the Supreme Court in J.M.H. v. K.H. [2015] IESC 85 , in which Charleton J. upheld an Isaac Wunder order in child-related proceedings, accepting evidence of an excessive number of applications brought by the father of the child as well as evidence of vexatious conduct. In M.M. v. G.M. [2015] IECA 29 , Kelly J. addressed a High Court order which directed that " no further application is to be made in respect of the children either by way of enforcement or review " before 26 March 2015. Despite the wide powers conferred on the courts by s. 11 of the Guardianship of Infants Act 1964 (as amended), Kelly J. found the order to violate constitutional norms and set aside the aspect of the order which purported to prohibit applications by way of enforcement or review in respect of the welfare of the children. The Attorney General submits that the case law reveals that ultimately, whether an order which denies a party access to the courts is to the benefit of the child and conforms with constitutional norms depends on the facts of each particular case. 

 Preliminary Discussion: Restrictions on the Right of Access to Justice 

 38.                  Article 40.3.1 ° of the Constitution provides: 

 "The State guarantees in its laws to respect, and, as far as practicable, by its laws to defend and vindicate the personal rights of the citizen." 

 39.                  It has long been recognised that one of the personal rights protected by the provisions of Article 40.3 is the right of access or recourse to the courts. This is the subject of a useful discussion in Kelly: The Irish Constitution (5 th ed., Bloomsbury Professional 2018) at para. 7.3.181 onwards. In the course of the discussion there, reference is made to cases such as Macauley v. Minister for Posts and Telegraphs [1966] I.R. 345, where Kenny J. said as follows at p. 358: 

 "That there is a right to have recourse to the High Court to defend and vindicate a legal right and that it is one of the personal rights of the citizen included in the general guarantee in Article 4, sect. 3, seems to me to be a necessary inference from Article 34, sect. 3, sub-sect. 1 ° ... 

 If the High Court has this full original jurisdiction to determine all matters and questions (and this includes the validity of any law having regard to the provisions of the Constitution), it must follow that the citizens have a right to have recourse to that Court to question the validity of any law having regard to the provisions of the Constitution or for the purpose of asserting or defending a right given by the Constitution, for if it did not exist, the guarantees and rights in the Constitution would be worthless." 

 40.                  Subsequently, it was noted in The State (McEldowney) v. Kelleher [1983] I.R. 289 by Costello J. in the High Court that there was also " the right to have recourse in appropriate cases to the District Court to defend or vindicate a legal right ". 

 41.                  There can be little or no doubt about the importance of access to justice for all individuals. Nevertheless, the fact that there is a right of access to justice does not mean that there can be no limits placed on an individual's right to litigate. At the heart of this case is the question of the extent to which limits can be placed on the right of access to the courts, and the jurisdiction of particular courts to make orders restricting such access. Litigation is generally a two-way process designed to determine disputes between parties who cannot resolve those disputes without access to justice.  Litigation arises in respect of many aspects of peoples' day-to-day lives, and a visit to the courts on any given day will demonstrate the vast variety of disputes that can arise between parties. The courts are charged with the administration of justice and will determine the liabilities of parties who come before them. In the normal course, that involves a hearing at first instance with the right of an appeal. That should normally be the end of the matter. 

 42.                  Bearing in mind that the right of access to justice is not unrestricted, it is necessary to consider the circumstances in which that right, fundamental and important as it may be, can be restricted. It is, perhaps, stating the obvious that in the course of litigation, it is inevitable that some parties will be dissatisfied with the outcome of the proceedings. As a general rule, a party dissatisfied with the outcome of litigation has a right of appeal. Assuming that a party has been unsuccessful at first instance, and thereafter unsuccessful on appeal, some will remain dissatisfied with the final outcome of the process of their litigation. However, it is also an important part of litigation that, having had a hearing at first instance, and thereafter an appeal, it is not open to a party to relitigate the same point in fresh proceedings. It will be readily apparent that an attempt to relitigate an issue that has already been decided will involve the use of further court time in relation to the new proceedings, and further, will put the successful party to the trouble of dealing yet again with proceedings raising the same issue. It is unfortunately the case that a small cohort of disappointed or unsuccessful litigants have sought to relitigate points already decided, again and again. Such behaviour gives rise to problems for the courts and for the parties at the receiving end of such litigation. Accordingly, such litigation has been the subject of a number of solutions, and it is the application of one of those solutions that is the subject of this appeal, namely, the use of what has come to be known as an Isaac Wunder order. 

 Isaac Wunder Case 

 43.                  Mr. Wunder brought a series of proceedings against Hospitals' Trust (1940) Limited which operated the Irish sweepstakes. Many of the tickets were sold in the United States where he resided, and Mr. Wunder embarked on a series of cases claiming that he had purchased the winning ticket. In each of the proceedings, he claimed that there had been negligence and a refusal on the part of the defendant to pay on the winning sweepstake ticket. In each instance, Mr. Wunder claimed that he had purchased the winning ticket in the sweepstake draw, that the prize money of £25,000 was not paid to him, and that if it was paid to any other person that was done by mistake, as he contended that he was the only winner who was entitled to the money. The judgment of the Supreme Court (O'Dálaigh CJ speaking for this Court)  on an appeal from a decision of the High Court recited as follows: 

 " Nor is this all. As Mr. Justice Murnaghan observed, this is the plaintiff's seventh action against the defendants in respect of alleged ownership of winning tickets in the Hospitals' Trust Sweepstake. The first five actions were in respect of 18 tickets, but at the trial the claim was reduced to 12 tickets. Mr. Justice O'Keeffe in a detailed and careful judgment pronounced each of these claims to be groundless; and this Court on appeal, after a careful re-examination of the proofs concurred fully in Mr. Justice O'Keeffe's Judgment. In giving the judgment of the Court, I said: "I cannot find in the plaintiff's case even a shadow of substance. If this case had been presented in Court by solicitor and counsel with the absence of proof which has marked the plaintiff's presentation the Court would find it hard to discover words to characterise their irresponsibility. The best that may be said of the plaintiff's several claims is that he has imagined them and now believes what he imagined. The defendants had no case to meet. They have, however, produced full and accurate records in respect of each claim made. This evidence shows that the plaintiff's several claims are, one and all, fantasy. It is due to the defendants that this should be said." 

 The plaintiff's sixth action came before Mr. Justice Henchy who dismissed it on the ground that it was frivolous and vexatious. The plaintiff's claim in that action was in respect of a prize-winning ticket No. XN05307 in the Sweepstake held on the 1950 Cambridgeshire. The plaintiff said he destroyed the ticket in Dublin in 1962 in circumstances which he purported to explain. The defendants from their records produced ticket No. XN05307 and the corresponding counterfoil, the latter bearing the following name and address of the subscriber: "Louis Jacobus, 264 Grove Avenue, Verona, N.Y." and, moreover, adduced proof of a claim by Mr. Jacobus in 1950 and payment to him in due course of the prize. 

 I said, delivering the judgment of this Court, "These documents can leave the Court in little doubt that the plaintiff's assertions with regard to ticket XN 05307 are shown to be groundless." The Court substituted an order in the form made by Mr. Justice Murnaghan in this present case for the order of dismissal which Mr. Justice Henchy has made. 

 I have taken the trouble to recount in detail the history of this litigation to demonstrate that there was no course open to Mr. Justice Murnaghan other than that which he took. 

 It is not in doubt that the plaintiff has become convinced of the justice of his claim in this case; but equally no member of this Court entertains any doubt that this claim has not been shown to have any foundation whatsoever. 

 One can only regret that the plaintiff should continue to waste his means in this irrational way; and one could wish that he would place his affairs in the hands of some friend or relative before he renders himself penniless by this pointless litigation. " 

 44.                  The order of Murnaghan J. was then affirmed. It should be noted that the order of Murnaghan J. which is recited by Ó Dálaigh C.J. in the course of the judgment is described as follows: " This is an appeal against an order of Murnaghan J. dated 6th February, ordering that no further proceedings should be taken in this action in the High Court without leave of that Court being first obtained and that if any such proceeding be taken in the action without such leave being first obtained the defendants should not be required to appear or take any steps in relation thereto and that such proceedings so taken should be treated as void and of no effect. " 

 45.                  Ó Dálaigh C.J. went on to explain that the order was made pursuant to a notice of motion brought by the defendants, " for an order that the action be stayed or dismissed on the grounds that it is frivolous and vexatious, or, alternatively, for an order that the summons therein should be struck out as disclosing no reasonable cause of action and for an order that the plaintiff be restrained from instituting proceedings against the defendants without the leave of the court. " 

 46.                  One might observe at the outset that the Wunder case was not one in which the plaintiff sought to relitigate the same point over and over again, as is often the case. Each case was brought by the plaintiff on the basis that he alleged that he had purchased a winning ticket in a sweepstake held on a particular race. As noted in the judgment of the Supreme Court, the first five actions brought by Mr. Wunder concerned 18 tickets, subsequently reduced to 12 tickets. There were then the proceedings before Henchy J. and proceedings before  Murnaghan J. in relation to other tickets. Thus, this is not, as I said, a case where the same point was sought to be re-litigated as such, but rather a case where the same litigant argued that he had won a prize in respective Irish sweepstakes. On each occasion, his claim related to a different event, and the defendants were able to demonstrate through their records that the prize had, in fact, been won by a different individual. There was, therefore, a series of cases making the same invalid point, albeit in relation to different events. It was in that context that the defendants sought to restrain Mr. Wunder from continuing to issue proceedings against them, and this was the order ultimately acceded to when the decision of Murnaghan J. in the High Court was upheld. It goes without saying that every time Mr. Wunder issued proceedings, the defendants were put to the trouble of being represented in the proceedings, and carrying out detailed searches of their records, which involved locating counterfoils from draws that had taken place sometimes many years earlier. Not surprisingly, they took steps to bring that course of conduct to an end, and having regard to the nature of the proceedings, the court restrained the commencement of further proceedings in accordance with the terms of the order that had been made by the High Court. It will be noted that the order was limited to the extent that Mr. Wunder was not allowed to issue proceedings without the leave of the High Court. It is also worth bearing in mind the comments made by Ó Dálaigh C.J. in the course of his judgment to the effect that the claims brought by Mr. Wunder " ha [d] not been shown to have any foundation whatsoever ". 

 47.                  It will have been observed that the defendants in those proceedings had brought a motion to dismiss the proceedings, or staying the proceedings, on the basis that they were frivolous and vexatious. The defendants had also sought, in the alternative, an order that the summons should be struck out as disclosing no reasonable cause of action and sought an order that the plaintiff be restrained from instituting proceedings against them without the leave of the court. 

 48.                  The jurisprudence in relation to the dismissal of proceedings, on the basis that they are frivolous or vexatious, or that they disclose no reasonable cause of action, was well-established by the time that the defendants in those proceedings brought their application. I will now  examine that process in more detail. 

   Limits on the right of access to justice 

 49.                  It should be reiterated that while there is a constitutional right of access to the courts, the right of access of a plaintiff to the court, as pointed out in Delany & McGrath on Civil Procedure (4 th ed, Round Hall, 2018) is something which has to be balanced " with the interests of defendants who should not be forced to defend proceedings that are vexatious or bound to fail" . The Rules of the Superior Courts have long reflected this necessity. Thus, O. 19, r. 27 of the RSC provides as follows: 

 " The Court may at any stage of the proceedings order to be struck out or amended any matter in any indorsement or pleading which is unnecessary or which amounts to an abuse of the process of the Court, or which may unreasonably prejudice or delay the fair trial of the action; and may in any such case, if it thinks fit, order the costs of the application to be paid as between solicitor and client. " 

 50.                  It will be observed immediately that the focus in O. 19, r. 27 is on the pleadings, and does not necessarily result in the striking out of the proceedings, but only that part of the pleadings which is " unnecessary ... or an abuse of the process of the Court ... ". Order 19, r. 28(1), which was recently amended by the Rules of the Superior Courts (Order 19) 2023 (S.I. No. 456 of 2023), provides as follows: 

 " The Court may, on an application by motion on notice, strike out any claim or part of a claim which: 

 (i)        discloses no reasonable cause of action, or 

 (ii)       amounts to an abuse of the process of the Court, or 

 (iii)      is bound to fail, or 

 (iv)       has no reasonable chance of succeeding. " 

 The balance of O. 19, r. 28, deals with the position in relation to defences. 

 51.                  While O. 19, r. 28 has been the subject of a recent amendment, it is fair to say that the present iteration is a reflection of the long-established case law in this area and as such represents a comprehensive expansion of the rules based power to strike out proceedings (see Kirwan v. Connors [2025] IESC 21 and in particular, the judgment of Hogan J. at paras 144-148). 

 52.                  Thus, it can be seen that the courts have always had provisions available to them in the Rules to enable litigation to be brought to a halt where it is clear that that litigation is frivolous and vexatious, or an abuse of the court. There are a number of other bases upon which the courts can dismiss proceedings which would otherwise be an abuse of process, but for the purpose of this judgment, I wish to focus on the jurisdiction of the courts to prevent an individual from issuing further proceedings where the party concerned has been involved in previously issuing what is found to be vexatious or frivolous litigation, or litigation which amounts to an abuse of process, without further leave of the court. 

 53.                  It is of interest to note that the application for relief in the Isaac Wunder case itself postdated the introduction of the 1962 iteration of O 19, r. 28 (Rules of the Superior Courts 1962, S.I. No. 72 of 1962). In considering whether a case is shown by its pleadings to be frivolous or vexatious, it is long established that the courts will examine the pleadings, and if it is concluded that a plaintiff " has no reasonable chance of succeeding then the law says that it is frivolous to bring the case. Similarly, it is a hardship on the defendant to have to take steps to defend something which cannot succeed and the law calls that vexatious ." ( Farley v. Ireland (Supreme Court, Barron J., 1 st May, 1997) at p. 3; see also paras. 16-09 to 16-11 of Delany & McGrath (4 th ed)). 

 Striking out proceedings pursuant to the inherent jurisdiction of the Court: Proceedings bound to fail 

 54.                  There was a further development in relation to proceedings which were deemed to be an abuse of process, or proceedings which were bound to fail. This topic was again discussed by the authors of Delany & McGrath (5 th ed., 2024), and in para. 16-38 they noted as follows: 

 "In Barry v. Buckley, Costello J. confirmed that a court has an inherent jurisdiction to strike out or stay proceedings if they are bound to fail. He explained that this "jurisdiction exists to ensure that an abuse of the process of the courts does not take place", and if the court was satisfied that the plaintiff's case must fail, "then it would be a proper exercise of its discretion to strike out proceedings whose continued existence cannot be justified and is manifestly causing irrevocable damage to the defendant." 

 55.                  It is useful to look at the judgment in that case in more detail ([1981] I.R. 306). Costello J. was considering circumstances in which a disappointed purchaser of land instituted proceedings for specific performance and registered a lis pendens against the land. However, on the facts as pleaded, it was established that no concluded agreement had been reached for the sale of the defendant's land to the plaintiff, and accordingly his claim was one which was bound to fail. At p. 308 of his judgment, Costello J. observed as follows: 

 "But, apart from Order 19, the Court has an inherent jurisdiction to stay proceedings and, on applications made to exercise it, the Court is not limited to the pleadings of the parties but is free to hear evidence on affidavit relating to the issues in the case: see: Wylie's Judicature Acts (1906) at pp. 34 - 37, and The Supreme Court Practice (1979) at para. 18/19/10. The principles on which the Court exercises its jurisdiction are well established. Basically its jurisdiction exists to ensure that an abuse of the process of the Courts does not take place. So, if the proceedings are frivolous or vexatious they will be stayed. They will also be stayed if it is clear that the plaintiff's claim must fail; per Buckley L.J. in Goodson v. Grierson at p. 765." 

 56.                  Costello J. went on to observe, in a passage which is often quoted, as follows: 

 "This jurisdiction should be exercised sparingly and only in clear cases; but it is one which enables the Court to avoid injustice, particularly in cases whose outcome depends on the interpretation of a contract or agreed correspondence. If, having considered the documents, the Court is satisfied that the plaintiff's case must fail, then it would be a proper exercise of its discretion to strike out proceedings whose continued existence cannot be justified and is manifestly causing irrevocable damage to a defendant." 

 57.                  He went on to make the observation that, in that particular case, an order could not have been made under O. 19, r. 28 as it then was, because of the circumstances of the case. In other words, on the pleadings, the plaintiff had made out a cause of action, but the court was requested, on the basis of the agreed facts established on affidavit, to exercise the court's inherent jurisdiction to strike out an action which must fail. Having considered the facts of the case, and having reached the conclusion that the facts did not establish " that a concluded bargain had been reached or confer on the plaintiff a right to specific performance ", he went on to observe as follows at p. 311: 

 "As the case is a clear one and as considerable injustice could result if the matter is not disposed of now, it seems that to allow the case to proceed to trial would be to permit an abuse of the Court's processes." 

 58.                  He, therefore, struck out the proceedings, and ordered that the lis pendens be vacated. That case is a very clear statement of the position vis- à -vis a court's jurisdiction to dismiss proceedings to ensure that an abuse of the process of the courts is not permitted. 

 59.                  This position was subsequently reiterated in the case of Keohane v. Hynes [2014] IESC 66 , at para. 6.5, by Clarke J. (as he then was) as follows: 

 "As pointed out in many of the authorities ... the underlying basis of the jurisdiction to dismiss as being bound to fail stems from the court's inherent entitlement to prevent an abuse of process. Bringing a case which is bound to fail is an abuse of process. If it is clear to a court that a case is bound to fail, then the court has jurisdiction to prevent that abuse of process by dismissing the proceedings." 

 60.                  Clarke J. went on to observe in that case at para. 6.6 that: 

 " [T] he jurisdiction is to be sparingly exercised and only adopted when it is clear that the proceedings are bound to fail rather than where the plaintiff's case is very weak or where it is sought to have an early determination on some point of fact or law." 

 See also the discussion on this issue in Delany & McGrath (5 th ed.), at paras. 16-38 et seq . 

 Abuse of Process: Further Consideration 

 61.                  The power to strike out proceedings on the basis that they constitute an abuse of process has long been established. Thus, in Fay v. Tegral Pipes Limited & Ors. [2005] 2 IR 261 , McCracken J. explained the jurisdiction of the court to dismiss proceedings as an abuse of process in the following terms: 

 "Such abuse cannot be permitted for two reasons. Firstly, the courts are entitled to ensure that the privilege of access to the courts, which is of considerable constitutional importance in relation to genuine disputes between parties, will only be used for the resolution of genuine disputes and not as a forum for lost causes which, no matter how strongly the party concerned may feel about them, nevertheless have no basis for a complaint in law. The second and equally important purpose of the jurisdiction is to ensure that litigants will not be subjected to the time consuming, expensive and worrying process of being asked to defend a claim which cannot succeed." 

 62.                  In their discussion on this issue, the authors of Delany & McGrath (5 th ed.) make the following comment, at para. 16-57: 

 "In his judgment in Doherty v. Minister for Justice, Equality & Law Reform, ( [2009] IEHC 246 , at para. 11) McGovern J. stated that he completely agreed with the dicta of McCracken J. in Fay v. Tegral Pipes Ltd and added that, "in addition to not permitting the courts to be a forum for lost causes, the courts should not be used to facilitate general abuse of a person, or class of persons". He stated that the courts are not to be used as a forum for ventilating complaints but rather for resolving genuine disputes between parties to litigation, and that "to permit the plaintiff's action to proceed would be to allow a parody of justice to take place". He concluded as follows: 

 Access to the courts is a constitutional right and entitles litigants to certain privileges. This carries with it certain obligations. That is why the courts will not permit abuse of process as to do so would bring the system of justice into disrepute. "   

 63.                  Thus, it can be seen that, apart from the procedures provided for in the RSC, which allow the striking out of proceedings on the grounds that they are frivolous or vexatious or do not disclose a cause of action, the courts have exercised the power to strike out proceedings which are an abuse of process, and in that regard have looked at a number of factors, including whether the proceedings are bound to fail, or as it was put by McCracken J. in Fay v. Tegral Pipe Limited , are " lost causes " which have no basis for a complaint in law. It has also been recognised that abuse of process has two aspects. In the first place, a case which involves an abuse of process will necessitate the use of court time to deal with a claim which has no basis and which, by its nature, involves a court employing resources that could be used for those with genuine disputes. The other aspect is the burden that such cases place on the opposing parties to the litigation. They are put to the expense, anxiety and trouble of defending such proceedings. The right to litigate and to have access to justice is an important constitutional right, but it is one that comes with obligations and should not be abused. The courts will endeavour to prevent such abuse. 

 64.                  Further, it should be noted that in the case of Aer Rianta c.p.t. v Ryanair Ltd. [2004] 1 IR 506 , Denham J. (as she then was), speaking for the court, observed at p. 509 of her judgment: 

 "The jurisdiction under O.19, r.28 to strike out pleadings is one a court is slow to exercise. A court will exercise caution in utilising this jurisdiction. However, if a court is convinced that a claim will fail such pleadings will be struck out." 

 65.                  For completeness, it should be observed that the striking out of cases as an abuse of process has occurred in cases where proceedings have been brought for an improper purpose, e.g., Sean Quinn Group Limited v. An Bord Pleanála & Ors. [2001] 1 I.R. 505, on the basis of unfounded allegations, and by reason of impropriety in the conduct of the proceedings, e.g. Farrell v. Bank of Ireland & Ors. [2012] IESC 42 ; [2015] IESC 71 . (For a comprehensive overview of the case law in this area, see paras. 16-70 to 16-84 of Delany & McGrath ). 

   

 66.                  While I have considered the development of the law in more recent years, it is worth recalling the earlier Rules of the Superior Courts issued in 1962 and the predecessor of the Rules found in O. 19, r. 28 of the Rules of the Supreme Court (Ireland) 1905. That Rule provided as follows: 

 "The Court or a Judge may, at any stage of the proceedings, order to be struck out or amended any matter in any indorsement or pleading which may be unnecessary or scandalous, or which may tend to prejudice, embarrass, or delay the fair trial of the action; and may in any such case, if they or he shall think fit, order the costs of the application to be paid as between solicitor and client." 

 67.                  As will be seen immediately, that Rule concerned the striking out of pleadings, as opposed to the proceedings themselves. There was a further provision contained in O. 25, r. 4 of the 1905 Rules, which is of relevance. It provides: 

 " The Court or a Judge may order any pleading to be struck out, on the ground that it discloses no reasonable cause of action or answer, and in any such case or in case of the action or defence being shown by the pleadings to be frivolous or vexatious, the Court or a Judge may order the action to be stayed or dismissed, or judgment to be ordered accordingly, as may be just ". 

 68.                  In The Judicature Acts (Ireland) and Rules of the Supreme Court (Ireland) 1905 ( Dublin: Sealy, Bryers and Walker, 1906) by James O. Wylie (" Wylie "), the following note appears in respect of O. 25, r. 4 : 

 "Applications under this rule must be tried upon the allegations contained in the pleadings: Attorney General v. London and N.W. RY. (1892) 3 Ch 274 ; but when application is made to the inherent jurisdiction of the Court to stay, dismiss, or strike out frivolous and vexatious actions or defences, evidence may be given: see Blair v. Cordner, 36 W.R. 64 ..." 

 69.                  A number of other cases are cited as authority for that proposition. As was observed in Wyley , applications are sometimes made under both headings. In other words, applications were made to strike out allegations in the pleadings, but also pursuant to the inherent jurisdiction of the court. 

 70.                  Reference was also made in Wylie to s. 27(5) of the Judicature Act (Ireland) 1877, which provided for the making of an order staying proceedings. In a note on the power conferred by s. 27(5), reference was made to circumstances in which frivolous and vexatious actions will be stayed (see pp. 34 - 35). It was noted further: 

 "On an application to stay proceedings as frivolous and vexatious and an abuse of process, the Judge cannot impose conditions on his assent or refusal: Bright v. Killy, 16 T.L.R. 559". 

 71.                  It is worth referring to two other situations referred to in Wylie at p. 35. It is stated: 

 "As to an order preventing any application in an action without leave, in order to stop repeated frivolous and vexatious applications, see, Kinnaird v. Field, W.N. 1905, 88. 

 Where seven actions were listed for hearing against same defendants, arising out of same facts, and two had been decided for defendants, the others were stayed until a new trial motion in one already decided should be determined in favour of plaintiff. O'Malley v. Steel, 26 I.L.T.R. 127". 

 72.                  Wylie went on to consider further examples of situations where proceedings would be stayed, for example, where two suits involved the same issue. 

 73.                  Thus, it can be seen that, although the order made in the Isaac Wunder case may be regarded as a "new" development in the law relating to vexatious litigation and abuse of process, it followed from a recognition by the courts, in legislation, and the Rules of the Superior Courts that vexatious litigation and abuse of process was a problem which required to be curtailed. 

 74.                  It would not be surprising to learn that the position in relation to vexatious or frivolous proceedings and abuse of process is mirrored in the jurisdiction of the courts of England and Wales. There are further developments in that jurisdiction to which I will refer later, but for the time being I propose to refer briefly to The Supreme Court Practice (1988): (Sweet & Maxwell Ltd, London, 1987), which refers to Order 18, Rule 19 of the Rules of the Supreme Court (S.I. 1965/1776) in that jurisdiction. (These rules were subsequently superseded by the Civil Procedure Rules 1998, S. I. 1998/3132.)  O.18, r. 19 is not dissimilar to our present iteration of O. 19, r. 28. It provided as follows: 

 "19. - The Court may at any stage of the proceedings order to be struck out or amended any pleading or the indorsement of any writ in the action, or anything in any pleading or in the indorsement, on the ground that  

 (a)  it discloses no reasonable cause of action or defence, as the case may be; or 

 (b)  it is scandalous, frivolous or vexatious; or 

 (c)  it may prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial of the action; or 

 (d)  it is otherwise an abuse of the process of the court; 

 and may order the action to be stayed or dismissed or judgment to be entered accordingly as the case may be." 

 75.                  O.18, r. 19(2) also provided that: 

 "No evidence shall be admissible on an application under paragraph 1(a)." 

 76.                  Commenting on the provisions of O. 18, r. 19, The Supreme Court Practice comments, at para. 18/19/1, as follows: 

 "Apart from the rule, the Court has an inherent jurisdiction to stay or dismiss actions, and to strike out pleadings which are vexatious or frivolous, or in any way an abuse of the process of the Court, under which it could deal with all the cases included in this rule (Reichel v. Magrath (1889) 14 App. Cas. 665; Remmington v. Scoles [1897] 2 Ch 1 , C.A.; Stevenson v. Garnett [1898] 1 QB 677 ). There has been a considerable extension in the inherent jurisdiction of the Court to protect itself from abuse. (Metrop Bank v. Pooley (1885) 10 App. Cas. 210). 

 77.                  On the subject of abuse of the process of the Court, The Supreme Court Practice had this to say at para. 18/19/17: 

 "Para. 1(d) confers upon the Court in express terms powers which the Court has hitherto exercised under its inherent jurisdiction where there appeared to be "an abuse of the process of the Court". This term connotes that the process of the Court must be used bona fide and properly and must not be abused. The Court will prevent the improper use of its machinery, and will, in a proper case, summarily prevent its machinery from being used as a means of vexation and oppression in the process of litigation. (See Castro v. Murray [1875] 10 Ex. 213; Dawkins v. Prince Edward of Saxe Weimar; Willis v. Earl Beauchamp (1886) 11 P. 59, per Bohan L.J. p.63). ..." 

 78.                  A number of examples are given of situations which amount to an abuse of process. For example, relitigating an identical question already decided against the party litigating, even though the matter is not strictly " res judicata ". Further, it is an abuse of the process of the Court to raise in subsequent proceedings matters which could and should have been litigated in earlier proceedings. It is also an abuse of process to allow proceedings to continue, even though the proceedings were viable when instituted, if by reason of subsequent events they have become inescapably doomed to failure, and as such they may be dismissed as being an abuse of the process of the court. Other examples are set out therein. 

 79.                  The Supreme Court Practice goes on to consider the inherent jurisdiction of the courts. In that context, at para. 18/19/18, it is observed: 

 " [T] he Court has an inherent jurisdiction to stay all proceedings before it which are obviously frivolous or vexatious or an abuse of its process. (See Reichel v. Magrath [1889] 14 App. Cas. 665)." 

 80.                  It can be seen therefore that, apart from the possibility of striking out part of the pleadings, the court could stay or dismiss actions which were found to be frivolous or vexatious. It was noted further that the power to stay or dismiss an action under the inherent jurisdiction of the court on the ground that it was obviously frivolous or vexatious is discretionary. The commentary went on to add that the inherent jurisdiction " is a most valuable adjunct to the powers conferred on the Court by these rules. When application is made to the inherent jurisdiction of the Court, all the facts can be gone into; and affidavits as to the facts are admissible ." 

 81.                  The observations continued by noting that: 

 " [I] f a party seeks to raise anew a question which has already been decided between the same parties by a Court of competent jurisdiction, this fact may be brought before the Court by affidavit, and the statement of claim, though good on the face of it, may be struck out, and the action dismissed; even though a plea of res judicata might not strictly be an answer to the action; it is enough if substantially the same point has been decided in a prior proceeding ...". 

 82.                  A number of cases were cited in support of that comment. Finally, it is noted in para. 18/19/18 that: 

 "In exceptional circumstances, the court has power to prohibit the plaintiff from bringing proceedings against others, unless the leave of the court is first obtained (Landi Den Hartog BV v. Sea Bird Limited [1976] F.S.R 489, harassing patent actions against the defendants' customers; and see Rose Records v. Motown Record Corporation [1983] F.S.R 361)." 

 83.                  It can be seen, therefore, that a similar consideration of the courts' functions in relation to vexatious or frivolous litigation or litigation that amounts to an abuse of the process of the courts has taken place in the courts of England and Wales, as outlined above, including to the extent of recognising the power to prohibit a party from bringing further proceedings without the leave of the court being first obtained. I will look at subsequent developments in that jurisdiction later in the course of this judgment. 

 Inherent Jurisdiction and Inherent Powers 

 84.                  For completeness, reference should be made to an interesting article, Inherent Jurisdiction and Inherent Powers of Irish Courts by Joan Donnelly in the Judicial Studies Institute Journal (2009) No. 2 at p. 122. In this article, the author makes the following observations at p. 127: 

 "The source of inherent jurisdiction in Ireland is the Constitution itself. Article 34.3.1 of the Constitution invests the High Court with "full original jurisdiction in and power to determine all matters and questions whether of law or fact, civil or criminal". It is by virtue of this article that the High Court hears common law actions, develops equitable doctrines and derives the authority to declare the rights and liabilities of individuals. 

 A power, on the other hand, is "an entitlement in law to use a procedural tool ... to hear and decide a cause of action in the Court within jurisdiction". An inherent power is exercisable by all courts. It is a power which is incidental and ancillary to the primary jurisdiction; the power is "parasitic" on the primary jurisdiction. Inherent powers are part of the common law of courts or, alternatively, arise by implication from the separation of powers doctrine. A court invokes its inherent power in order to fulfil its constitutionally-ordained function as a court of law and to accomplish the administration of justice in a regular, orderly and effective manner." 

 85.                  The distinction made by the author between inherent jurisdiction and inherent powers is of some significance, and it appears that the phrase " inherent jurisdiction " is frequently used in superior court judgments when that which is being exercised is more properly referred to as an " inherent power ". 

 86.                  In her article, Ms. Donnelly identifies a number of matters which she says are clearly categories of inherent jurisdiction, including parens patriae , judicial review, setting aside of unsound judgments, punishing for contempt, and variation of trusts, amongst others. 

 87.                  There then follows an interesting discussion on the source of inherent powers of courts. One theory posited is that they are " derived from the common law " and the alternative is that they are implied by the doctrine of the separation of powers. In this context, she refers to the comments by Murray J. in the case of GMcG v. DW (No. 2) [2000] 4 I.R. 1, in which he characterises inherent powers as necessarily accruing to a court by virtue of " the very nature of its judicial function or its constitutional role in the administration of justice ". The author goes on to observe that many inherent powers developed by the courts are now codified in court rules, and to that extent she argues that inherent powers supplement the court rules. 

 88.                  The author then goes on to refer to a number of inherent powers that have arisen in the Irish context, and she describes those as: 

 " (a)            Power of court to regulate its own procedure and protect fair trial process; 

 (b)       Power to prevent steps being taken that would render judicial proceedings inefficacious; 

 (c)        Power to prevent abuse of process; and 

 (d)       Power to act in aid of Superior Courts and in aid or control of inferior courts. " 

 89.                  Regardless of the classification of those matters said to be part of the inherent jurisdiction of the courts and those which are said to be inherent powers of the courts, it could be observed that a court which is dependent on statute for its jurisdiction could enjoy only that jurisdiction which is so provided. Thus, the argument goes that the District Court and the Circuit Court, being creatures of statute, do not enjoy an inherent jurisdiction such as that which is enjoyed by the High Court, which is a court of full and original jurisdiction pursuant to Art. 34.3.1 ° of the Constitution. That proposition must be correct. One might argue that the classification of matters that fall into the category of inherent jurisdiction and inherent powers does not, in fact, reflect necessarily the full extent of what is or is not captured by the concept of inherent jurisdiction. For example, the categorisation of the contempt of court jurisdiction as arising from the inherent jurisdiction of the courts is something that seems difficult to reconcile with the general proposition that inherent powers are there to assist courts in regulating their own processes and preventing abuse of court processes. In this context, it is interesting to note the views of the Law Reform Commission. In its Issues Paper on Contempt of Court and Other Offences and Torts involving the Administration of Justice (LRC IP 10 - 2016), the Commission described the complexities of the law in relation to contempt of court. It noted at para. 1.14 that: 

 " The High Court has full jurisdiction to deal with all forms of contempt and may exercise jurisdiction concerning contempt of the Circuit Court and the District Court. The Circuit Court and District Court have the power to deal summarily with contempt in the face of the court but "beyond that the position is less clear." In its Consultation Paper on Contempt of Court, the Commission noted that "it is particularly doubtful whether the District Court's jurisdiction extends to such matters as the sub judice rule."
