The Commission recommended in its subsequent Report on Contempt of Court that the Circuit Court and District Court should have the same jurisdiction as the High Court in contempt proceedings, but where the punishment involves the imposition of a fine, this should be subject to monetary limits. This recommendation (along with the other recommendations in the 1994 Report) has not been implemented and so there is still uncertainty in this area." 

 90.                  This is not the place in which to engage in a full overview of the law of contempt. It is, however, worth noting the categorisation of the forms of contempt set out by the Law Reform Commission at para. 1.06 of its Issues Paper as follows: 

 " Criminal contempt can take the form of: 

 ·          contempt in the face of the court (contempt in facie curiae ), which comprises conduct that deliberately disrupts or obstructs court proceedings and is prejudicial to the course of justice; 

 ·          scandalising the court, making or publishing untrue allegations about a court or judge that would undermine public confidence in the judiciary; and 

 ·          sub judice contempt, publishing prejudicial material about pending court proceedings that would interfere with the administration of justice. " 

 91.                  A description is also given of civil contempt, and it is noteworthy that, for example, the Circuit Court Rules contain provisions in relation to attachment and committal, which are designed to deal with those who refuse to comply with court orders (see Order 37 in particular). The Circuit Court has jurisdiction to deal with criminal contempt in general but there may be some issues concerning the full extent of this jurisdiction 

 92.                  It should be noted that extensive provisions are set out in the Courts (Supplemental Provisions) Act 1961 as to the jurisdiction of the Circuit Court. In this regard, see s. 22 of that Act. Of particular interest are the provisions of s. 22(6) and (7). These provisions provide: 

 "(6)     The Circuit Court, as regards any cause of action for the time being within its jurisdiction, shall in any proceedings before it - 

 (a)       grant such relief, redress or remedy or combination of remedies, absolute or conditional, and 

 (b)       give such and the like effect to every ground of defence or counterclaim, legal or equitable, 

 as ought to be granted or given in the like case by the High Court and in as full and ample a manner. 

 (7)       Without prejudice to any jurisdiction conferred by the previous subsections of this section, the Circuit Court shall have powers of attachment, garnishee and interpleader, and shall have all powers (including the power to appoint a receiver) ancillary to any jurisdiction exercisable by it." 

 This provision will be considered further below. 

 93.                  As mentioned above, this judgment is not the place to set out in full the extent of the jurisdiction of the Circuit Court in relation to matters such as contempt of court, or indeed the jurisdiction of the District Court in this respect. However, the jurisdiction of those courts to deal with, for example, contempt in the face of the court cannot be doubted, and while the source of the jurisdiction to make such orders may be the subject of academic discussion, it would be difficult to argue against the proposition that inherent to the proper functioning of any court is the power to take action to protect that court from instances of criminal contempt which have the effect of disrupting the administration of justice. It would be a surprising conclusion if, in fact, it was said that those courts did not have the power in furtherance of the administration of justice to deal with contempt. 

 94.                  Leaving aside the issue of contempt, the author of the article referred to above places powers such as the power to dismiss a claim for want of prosecution, or the power to grant a stay of proceedings, in the category of inherent powers. (It should be noted that an interesting discussion of "inherent jurisdiction" as opposed to "procedural powers" is to be found in the judgment of Murray J. in the case of Kirwan v Connors referred to above at paras. 18 - 33.)  This case is concerned with the inherent power of a court to regulate the proceedings before it in order to prevent what might otherwise become an abuse of that court's process. This brings me to a consideration of the specific issues arising in this appeal. 

 The Making of Isaac Wunder Orders in Family Law Proceedings 

 95.                  The first question to be determined in these proceedings concerns the entitlement of a court to make an Isaac Wunder order in family law proceedings. It is ironic that the first suggestion of the making of an Isaac Wunder order was, in fact, made by the appellant in the Circuit Court as an alternative to the making of a Costs Order against him. The Circuit Court then made such an order (see para. 5 above). Further, when the matter was before the Court of Appeal, the appellant agreed to the Court considering afresh the making of an Isaac Wunder order (see para. 6 of the judgment of Woulfe J.). Indeed, it is now the position of the appellant, as was conceded in his oral submissions before this Court, that an Isaac Wunder order could be made in family law proceedings. The focus of his argument during the hearing before this Court concerned whether the making of such an order is proportionate in the circumstances, and he argued that, before making such an order, less restrictive measures should be used first. In a reply to the request for clarification issued by this Court, this is what was said by the appellant in that context: 

 "The appellant submits that the court should always begin by applying less restrictive measures in these circumstances if resorting to an Isaac Wunder Order. In other words, courts should apply the least restrictive means necessary to achieve the legitimate aim of preventing abuse of litigation, while balancing the rights of the parties and ensuring that the best interests of the child remain paramount." 

 The Best Interests of the Child 

 96.               Article 42A.1 provides as follows: 

 "The State recognises and affirms the natural and imprescriptible rights of all children and shall, as far as practicable, by its laws protect and vindicate those rights." 

 97.               Article 42A.4.1° is also of relevance: 

 "1.      Provision shall be made by law that in the resolution of all proceedings - 

 i           brought by the State, as guardian of the common good, for the purpose of preventing the safety and welfare of any child from being prejudicially affected, or 

 ii          concerning the adoption, guardianship or custody of, or access to, any child, the best interests of the child shall be the paramount consideration." 

 98.               The Constitution goes on to provide for provision to be made for hearing the voice of the child. 

 99.               Since the insertion of Article 42A into the Constitution, its provisions have been considered in a number of cases, including Re JB and KB [2018] IESC 30 , [2019] 1 IR 270 , and In the Matter of JJ [2021] IESC 1 , [2022] 3 I.R. 1. Much of the focus of Article 42A was on the circumstances in which the State could intervene to protect the safety and welfare of a child in circumstances where the parent or parents of the child had failed in this regard. There is a detailed discussion in the case of In the Matter of JJ about the scope of Article 42A (see paras. 124 et seq .). In the course of the passage on Article 42A, the following is said at para. 131: 

 "131.   In some aspects, most notably in the recognition of the rights of children contained in Article 42A.1, it can be said that the change was one of emphasis rather than substance, or making explicit what was implicit, but that does not mean that the change was without significance or importance for constitutional interpretation. The Constitution has, since 1937, affirmed the central importance of the Family. The Family is, however, a collective body made up of individuals who themselves have rights. One aspect of the constitutional position of the Family is the right of a family collectively to make decisions, for example, in relation to lifestyle or life choices, sometimes as a result of religious or ethical beliefs, and the State must respect those choices within certain constitutional limits. However, some decisions made within the Family are decisions by parents in relation to their children, and where it is possible that the parental decision, or the absence of a parental decision can be said to be damaging to the interests of the child. Article 42A.1 is an emphatic statement of the rights of the child, and that there is, therefore, a corresponding duty on parents to uphold and vindicate those rights. 

 132.     The question of medical treatment, of which this case is one dramatic example, is one area which can pose distinct problems. That is because parental decisions in relation to medical treatment are not necessarily an example of collective family decision-making about life choices. It may simply be that, as a matter of common law, any medical procedure requires the patient's consent, and that, since a child cannot lawfully provide such consent, a substitute consent is necessary. In such circumstances, the rights of the child come to the forefront. One of the objectives of Article 42A.1, and the express statement of the rights of the child, is, perhaps, to ensure that such cases were not approached by reference to the objective of maintaining the authority of the family, but rather through the lens of the rights of the child. 

 133.     The constitutional Amendment embodied in Article 42A is subtle but its direction is clearly discernible. It seeks to maintain the essential structure of the Constitution and a balance - and, in some cases, a necessary tension - between the position and autonomy of the Family vis-à-vis the State, and the rights of an individual child. It also retains important parts of the language of Article 42.5 in its reference to and emphasis on the "natural and imprescriptible rights of all children", and in its provision that the State may supply the position of parents only in "exceptional circumstances", where there is something which can be properly described as "a failure" of parental duty. The use of language emphasises the fact that there must remain a significant and high threshold before the State can override parental decision-making." 

 100.           It will be apparent from those passages that the primary focus of Article 42A is on the circumstances in which the State can intervene where there has been a failure in the duty of parents towards their children, insofar as their safety or welfare is likely to be prejudicially affected (see Article 42A.2.1 ° ). 

 101.           It is interesting to note the observations contained in Kelly: The Irish Constitution (5 th ed.) on the subject of the best interests test at para. 7.7.207, at which it is stated as follows: 

 " By virtue of Article 42A.4.1 ° , provision must be made by law that in proceedings concerning the adoption, guardianship or custody of, or access to a child, or proceedings taken by the State seeking to protect the safety and welfare of any child, the best interests of the child shall be the paramount consideration. 

 Proceedings concerning applications for asylum or the deportation of a child do not come within the scope of Article 42A.4. However, the courts must have regard to the constitutional rights of children in any legal proceedings where those rights are relevant. " 

 102.           The respondent in her submissions made the point that the reliance of the appellant on Article 42A was focused on his right of access to the courts. In other words, the arguments of the appellant suggest that the best interests of the child are only met by allowing him access to the courts. She points out that litigation in family law proceedings that is prolonged and vexatious unnecessarily causes a number of problems for the child. It increases acrimony between the parents, causes avoidable distress, and has negative impacts on the financial resources of the parent at the receiving end of such unmeritorious and vexatious litigation. 

 103.           One observation should be made in relation to the focus of the appellant on the provisions of Article 42A.4.1 ° . It is expressly provided therein that " Provision shall be made by law that in the resolution of all proceedings ... the best interests of the child shall be the paramount consideration ." The words "provision shall be made by law " should be noted. No such provision has been made to date which could have a bearing on these proceedings. Nevertheless, in this context, it is relevant to note the judgment in AZ v Minister for Justice [2024] IESC 35 in which Woulfe J. considered the distinction between Art. 42A.1 and Art. 42A.4. He observed at paras.101-102 of the judgment in that case as follows: 

 "101.    Firstly, approaching the issue from first principles, Article 42A. 1 is of general application so that the rights of an Irish citizen child, including the welfare of the child, require consideration when the Minister is making deportation decisions which may seriously affect the child. It seems to me that the obligation placed on the courts to have regard to Article 42A.1 of the Constitution, as referred to by Murray J in Sivsivadze and set out at para.78 above, is of very wide application and includes application to these types of immigration decisions which may seriously affect children. In my opinion the Minister is under a similar obligation by virtue of Article 42A.1 to take appropriate account of these welfare considerations. In the present case this meant that she was required to take account of the special circumstances arising, with the father being the principal care giver of a child with very special needs. 

 102.     Secondly, I do not accept the Minister's submissions that the trial judge in substance found, without expressly finding, that Article 42A .4 does apply to immigration matters, and that her judgement appears to conflate Article 42 A .1 with Article 42 A .4. In my opinion, Phelan J clearly recognise the limitations inherent in the latter provision (such as the reference only to certain types of proceedings), and she relied instead on the general applicability of the former provision, for example at paras 100 and 105 of her judgement. I might add that, as per the judgement of this court in In re JJ (at paragraph 141), Article 42A .4 .1 appears to me to be a mandatory provision obliging the State to legislate to provide for a certain principle in certain types of proceedings involving a child. However, this latter provision can be seen as really a type of lex specialis which does not take from the general applicability of the former provision." 

 This is a useful overview of the provisions of Article 42A. However, turning back to the issue in this case, it is hard to see how the pursuit of endless litigation by one party against another parent in family law proceedings could be justified by reliance on " the best interests of the child ". Indeed, the opposite could be the case. Pursuing another parent endlessly through the courts to re-argue decisions that have been made as to custody, access or maintenance when there is no need to do so is simply not appropriate. It could hardly be said to be in the best interests of the child either. The stress, strain and expense caused to a party who is subjected to constant applications will undoubtedly have some adverse effect on the child concerned, particularly if the child is subject to repeated examinations of psychiatrists or psychologists in the context of access or custody disputes.  If it was truly necessary and proper to bring proceedings relating to custody, access or maintenance in respect of a child by reason of a change in circumstances, then there would be no inhibition in bringing such proceedings. Even if an Isaac Wunder order had previously been made against a parent in family law proceedings, if a material change occurred giving rise to a need for a further application to court, then, no doubt, a court would give leave to pursue those proceedings. However, for my part, I cannot see how the constitutional provisions in relation to the best interests of the child set out in Article 42A of the Constitution can avail a party who has engaged in vexatious and abusive litigation to continue to do so by reference to the best interests of the child. In my view, such an argument is misplaced. 

 Further Aspects of the Right of Access to the Courts 

 104.           The point was made on behalf of the appellant that any interference with the right of access to the courts must be proportionate, and in this context, reliance was placed on Heaney v. Ireland [1994] 3 I.R. 593 to make the point that any interference with the constitutional right of access to the courts must " impair the right as little as possible ". That, of course, is so, but as mentioned above, the right of access to the courts must be balanced with the right of other parties who are brought to court as defendants not to be the subject of vexatious litigation or litigation that is bound to fail, on a repeated basis. 

 105.           The appellant also asserted rights of access to the courts by reference to the Convention. In this context, reference was made to Article 6 (Right to a Fair Trial) and Article 8 (Right to Respect for Private and Family Life) of the Convention and to a number of decisions of the European Court of Human Rights in the context of proceedings concerning parental access. Thus, reference was made to A.D. and O.D. v. The United Kingdom ( App. No. 28680/06, 16 th June, 2010) , where it was held by the ECtHR as follows: 

 " A stricter scrutiny is called for, however, in respect of any further limitations, such as restrictions placed by those authorities on parental rights of access (see, for example, T.P. and K.M. v. the United Kingdom [GC], no. 28945/95, paras. 71 to 72, ECHR 2001‑V (extracts)). " (para. 83) 

 106.           The appellant also referred to the decision in the case of Elsholz v. Germany (App. No. 25735/94, 13 th July, 2000) in which it was stated: 

 " 49.     The margin of appreciation to be accorded to the competent national authorities will vary in accordance with the nature of the issues and the importance of the interests at stake. Thus, the Court recognises that the authorities enjoy a wide margin of appreciation, in particular when assessing the necessity of taking a child into care. However, a stricter scrutiny is called for in respect of any further limitations, such as restrictions placed by those authorities on parental rights of access, and of any legal safeguards designed to secure an effective protection of the right of parents and children to respect for their family life. Such further limitations entail the danger that the family relations between the parents and a young child would be effectively curtailed. ... " 

 107.           The decision in the case of T.P. and K.M. v. The United Kingdom (App. No. 28945/95, 10 th May, 2001) was also referred to in which it was held as follows: 

 "70.     In determining whether the impugned measures were "necessary in a democratic society", the Court will consider whether, in the light of the case as a whole, the reasons adduced to justify them were relevant and sufficient for the purposes of paragraph 2 of Article 8 of the Convention. Undoubtedly, consideration of what lies in the best interest of the child is of crucial importance in every case of this kind. ... 

 72.  The Court further recalls that whilst Article 8 contains no explicit procedural requirements, the decision-making process involved in measures of interference must be fair and such as to afford due respect to the interests safeguarded by Article 8: 

 "[W]hat has to be determined is whether, having regard to the particular circumstances of the case and notably the serious nature of the decisions to be taken, the parents have been involved in the decision-making process, seen as a whole, to a degree sufficient to provide them with the requisite protection of their interests. If they have not, there will have been a failure to respect their family life and the interference resulting from the decision will not be capable of being regarded as 'necessary' within the meaning of Article 8. (see the W. v. the United Kingdom judgment of 8 July 1987, Series A no. 121-A, pp. 28-29, paras. 62 and 64)." 

 108.           The respondent in her submissions made a number of points in response to the appellant's reliance on these decisions of the ECtHR. In the first instance, the point was made that the making of an Isaac Wunder order in maintenance and child access proceedings was not the curtailment of " relations between the parents and a young child " in the sense expressed by the ECtHR in Elsholz , nor an " interference " in the appellant's family life, as that phrase is used in T.P. v. The United Kingdom . As was pointed out, the issue in Elsholz involved a situation where the domestic courts had violated an applicant's Article 8 right to family life by refusing to grant him any access to his child. The decision had been made without obtaining an independent psychological report, and without sufficiently involving the applicant in the hearing that led to the decision. T.P. involved similar issues regarding the unfairness of process that was found to have occurred in that case. 

 109.           In my view, these cases concern an entirely different situation to that which pertains here. There is no suggestion here that the appellant has been deprived of a right to participate fully in the proceedings concerning access to his child or on the issue of maintenance, and he has done so on many occasions. Nor is it a case where a decision has been made by a court without his knowledge or active participation. What is at issue here is the pursuit of litigation on a constant basis by the appellant, which is said to be without merit, vexatious and an abuse of process 

 110.           It will be seen, therefore, that there is nothing in the jurisprudence of the European Court of Human Rights that prohibits or prevents restrictions being placed on an individual's right of access to the courts in appropriate circumstances. Of course, the restriction of a right of access to court is a serious step not to be undertaken lightly and that, of course, is a proposition that underlies the making of an Isaac Wunder order in this jurisdiction. The ECtHR  pointed out that any such restriction " must pursue a legitimate aim and there must be a reasonable relationship of proportionality between the means employed and the aim sought to be achieved ." ( Tolstoy Miloslavsky v. United Kingdom , para. 59). 

 111.           I have no difficulty in agreeing with the general proposition, that family law proceedings are particularly sensitive for all concerned and that attention must be paid to the best interests of children caught up in such proceedings. Nevertheless, it does not follow that the courts do not enjoy the same powers to control such proceedings and prevent abuse of their process as they do in other civil law proceedings. It was urged on this Court by the appellant that while courts involved in family law proceedings have a jurisdiction to restrain vexatious and unmeritorious litigation, extra caution and care should be taken in family law matters due to their nature and the inherent differences with other forms of civil dispute. 

 112.           Relying on this contention, the appellant has posited that a different approach should be adopted in this jurisdiction akin to that which pertains elsewhere, notably, the jurisdiction to make civil restraint orders in England and Wales. Setting out the history behind such orders, reference was made to the decision in Bhamjee v. Forsdick (No. 2) [2004] 1 WLR 88 . In that case, it was observed at para. 11 as follows: 

 " The power to protect its processes from abuse is vested in every court. The starting point is the judgment of Baron Alderson in Cocker v Tempest (1840-41) 7 M&W 501: 

 "The power of each court over its own process is unlimited; it is a power incident to all courts, inferior as well as superior; were it not so, the court would be obliged to sit still and see its own process abused for the purpose of injustice. The exercise of the power is certainly a matter for the most careful discretion. "" 

 113.           It was then observed at para. 16 as follows: 

 " This court, therefore, like any court, has an inherent jurisdiction to protect its processes from abuses of this kind. The next question is to determine what measures are appropriate for this purpose. It is now well settled both at common law and under Strasbourg jurisprudence that a court has power to regulate its affairs in such a way that its processes are not abused. " 

 114.           The court went on to refer to, inter alia , the case of Tolstoy-Miloslavsky , referred to above, and continued as follows: 

 "These cases proclaim the message that the right of access to the courts may be subject to limitations in the form of regulation by the state, so long as two conditions are satisfied: 

 (i)                  the limitations applied do not restrict or reduce the access left to the individual in such a way or to such an extent that the very essence of the right is impaired; 

 (ii)               a restriction must pursue a legitimate aim and there must be a reasonable relationship of proportionality between the means employed and the aim sought to be achieved." 

 115.           The Court then made reference to the case of Ebert v. Venvil [2000] Ch 484 , in which Lord Woolf MR said of Article 6 at 497 as follows: 

 "Article 6 does no more than reflect the approach of the common law indicated by Laws J. in Reg v. Lord Chancellor, Ex parte Witham [1998] QB 575 . As long as the inherent power is exercised only when it is appropriate for it to be exercised, no contravention of article 6 or common law principle is involved." 

 116.           One further passage from Ebert v Venvil is of interest . where it was observed at p. 498: 

 "The High Court has traditionally exercised a supervisory jurisdiction in relation to the county court and although that jurisdiction is normally exercised over the county court by means of judicial review this does not mean that it is the only way the jurisdiction can be exercised. It could for example properly be exercised by the granting of an injunction or by the sort of orders made by Neuberger J. If authority was needed for this it is provided in re Connolly Brothers Ltd. [1911] 1 Ch 731 . In that case the proceedings which were restrained were in the Lancaster Palatine Court and not a county court. In addition the proceedings had already been commenced when they were restrained. Furthermore the injunction would be enforceable against the individual and not the court. None the less these distinctions do not alter the principle involved. The county court,will give effect to the High Court order in the same way as it would give effect to an order made by a county court judge. We still have a High Court and county courts with separate but overlapping jurisdictions. However both courts are part of the same civil justice system."   

 I would pause here to observe that the origins of the supervisory jurisdiction of the High Court in that jurisdiction and the supervisory role of the High Court in this jurisdiction in respect of the Circuit and District Courts are not necessarily the same. In this jurisdiction, q uite apart from the fact that the pre-1922 High Court enjoyed a power at common law to supervise and correct inferior courts such as the then County Court, the hierarchical nature of the court system provided for by the Constitution clearly implies the High Court has a similar supervisory jurisdiction in respect of the Circuit Court and the District Court. While the High Court has a full original jurisdiction as provided for by Article 34.3.1⁰, the Circuit Court and District Courts are designated as courts of local and limited jurisdiction for the purposes of Article 34.3.4⁰. This constitutional structure clearly suggests that the High Court can act in aid of these courts of local and limited where it is necessary to protect and conserve the administration of justice as envisaged by Article 34.1 from abuse. 

 117.           In Bhamjee , the Court also cited the provisions of s. 42 of the Supreme Court Act 1981 (now known as the Senior Courts Act 1981), which provides for the making of orders restraining vexatious litigants. It is interesting to note some of the features of that jurisdiction, which are set out in para. 20 of the judgment therein. So, for example, a civil proceedings order can only be made on the application of the Attorney General. Such orders remain in force indefinitely unless otherwise provided. A copy of the order is required to be published in the London Gazette. Further, once the Court has made a civil proceedings order, the order regulates the litigant's right of access not only to the High Court, but also to the Court of Appeal and the County Court. 

 118.           Commenting on the effect of an order made under s .42, the following was said at para. 24: 

 " A section 42 order has been described as a draconian order. It covers all the litigation and all the applications a vexatious litigant may wish to bring, and if a High Court judge refuses permission in relation to any attempt the litigant may wish to make to bring a matter to the attention of a court that is the end of the matter. It involves the publication of the litigant's name on a list which receives widespread circulation, and although some recent orders have been made for a fixed period of time, by January 2000 only one ten-year order and one 15-year order had fallen into this category (see Attorney-General v Ebert (COT 7th July 2000) per Silber J at paras 55-57). It is therefore a form of relief which has a long term effect. " 

 119.           The interaction between the statutory jurisdiction, on the one hand, and the inherent jurisdiction, which would be akin to our Isaac Wunder jurisdiction and is comparable to the Grepe v Loam ( [1887] 37 Ch D 168 ) jurisdiction in England and Wales, was also considered. The decision of Lord Woolf MR in Ebert v. Venvil , to which reference has already been made was referred to once more: 

 " This is one of the situations where it is accepted that notwithstanding the intervention of Parliament an inherent jurisdiction remains alongside the statutory jurisdiction. This does not mean that intervention of Parliament may not have cut down the inherent jurisdiction of the court. If there was an application for an order of the same width as the statutory jurisdiction, the court could only appropriately deal with such an application under the statutory jurisdiction. The inherent jurisdiction to make an order is now more restricted. The question is how much more restricted. " (at p. 493) 

 120.           It was then noted that Grepe v. Loam orders could be made in courts other than the Queen's Bench Division, including a county court, in the exercise of its inherent jurisdiction to protect its process from abuse. The Court in Bhamjee proceeded in the course of its judgment to rename what were then known as Grepe v. Loam orders as 'civil restraint orders.' The Court in that case went on to consider the forms of civil restraint orders that might be made in an appropriate case. The Court imposed certain temporal limits in relation to such orders before making a more extended long-term form of order. 

 121.           Of particular significance, from the point of view of the appellant herein, was the step-by-step approach advocated by the Court of Appeal in that case. In particular, reliance is placed on para. 54 of the judgment, where it was stated as follows: 

 "In conclusion, the nuisance described in Bhamjee (No 1) is now such that we consider that the time has come when the courts should make use of their inherent jurisdiction to control it. Strasbourg jurisprudence requires the responses of the courts to be proportionate, and we consider that the two year civil restraint orders of the type we have described in this judgment represent the kind of step by step process approved by Strasbourg jurisprudence which may ultimately end, if the vexatious litigant's conduct is not only persistent but also habitual, in the making of a long term s 42 order. The inherent jurisdiction of the court has always existed side by side with its rule-derived jurisdiction (see now CPR 3.1(1)), and the Rules Committees will no doubt wish to consider in due course whether it would be desirable to exercise their rule-making powers in this regard. All we are doing in this judgment is to provide a modern incarnation of the protection described by Bowen LJ in Willis v Earl Beauchamp [1886] 11 PD 59 in these words: 

 "...  The rules ... do not ... deprive the court in any way of the inherent power which every court has to prevent the use of legal machinery which will occur, if for no possible benefit the defendants are to be dragged through litigation which must be long and expensive." 

 Today it is also the resources of the courts themselves that require protection." 

 122.           It is interesting to observe the manner in which the inherent power of the courts to regulate their own procedures in that jurisdiction have been added to by statutory provisions, alongside common law developments to the courts' inherent power, having had regard to the need for proportionality and to the jurisprudence of the ECtHR. 

 123.           It can also be noted that in other jurisdictions, such as Canada and Australia, statutory provisions have been introduced to set out the manner in which courts should deal with vexatious litigants. 

 124.           The respondent in her submissions referred to the later decision of Nowak v. The Nursing and Midwifery Council [2013] EWHC 1932 (QB) at paras. 58 to 59, in which Leggatt J. said as follows: 

 "58.     As explained by the Court of Appeal in the leading case of Bhamjee v Forsdick [2003] EWCA Civ 1113 , [2004] 1 WLR 88 , the rationale for the regime of civil restraint orders is that a litigant who makes claims or applications which have absolutely no merit harms the administration of justice by wasting the limited time and resources of the courts. Such claims and applications consume public funds and divert the courts from dealing with cases which have real merit. Litigants who repeatedly make hopeless claims or applications impose costs on others for no good purpose and usually at little or no cost to themselves. Typically, such litigants have time on their hands and no means of paying any costs of litigation - so they are entitled to remission of court fees and the prospect of an order for costs against them is no deterrent. In these circumstances there is a strong public interest in protecting the court system from abuse by imposing an additional restraint on their use of the court's resources. 

 59.       It is important to note that a civil restraint order does not prohibit access to the courts. It merely requires a person who has repeatedly made wholly unmeritorious claims or applications to have any new claim or application which falls within the scope of the order reviewed by a judge at the outset to determine whether it should be permitted to proceed. The purpose of a civil restraint order is simply to protect the court's process from abuse, and not to shut out claims or applications which are properly arguable." 

 125.           Reliance was also placed on the decision in the case of A.E.Y. v. A.L. [2018] EWHC 3253 (Fam) in which a civil restraint order was made in the context of family law proceedings and that order was then extended in view of multiple applications for leave to appeal made by the father in that case. As was noted in that case by Knowles J. at para. 68: 

 "I acknowledge that such orders are not commonly made in the context of children proceedings given the availability of section 91(14) orders to restrain applications in such proceedings. Nevertheless, they are available to the court in certain circumstances and, in my view, are a useful means of protecting the family justice system from the abuse identified in the case of Nowak. I have clarified with the Family Court that the father is presently not subject to either an order pursuant to section 91(14) of the Children Act 1989 or to any form of civil restraint order." 

 126.           While it was accepted by the respondent that Article 42A necessitates a more " child-centred approach ", by virtue of making the child's best interests the " paramount consideration " in any civil proceedings concerning adoption, guardianship or custody it was argued that, given that the rights at issue essentially concern the child's right to enjoy a relationship with his father, even in circumstances where an Isaac Wunder order has been made, the rights of the child to have access to and a relationship with his father are not hindered by the making of such an order where an application can be made to the President of the Court (or a judge nominated by the President) for leave to bring a further application. When any such application for leave is required to be made, the judge dealing with the matter will have to consider all of the rights affected by the Isaac Wunder order, and the proposed further application. These include the rights of the child to have a relationship with the non-custodial parent, but also the rights of the custodial parent to be spared the burden of the effects of unjust and abusive litigation, whether that is litigation which is unjustly prolonged,  costly, or vexatious. Such a court would have to consider the nature of the proposed further litigation and the potential effects on the rights of all those concerned and affected by it. 

 127.           In the course of his submissions, the Attorney General referred to a number of authorities in relation to the inherent powers of courts to protect the court process. Reference was made, for example, to the decision of the Supreme Court in Riordan v. Ireland (No. 4) [2001] 3 IR 365 at p. 370, where it was stated that there was vested in the Supreme Court, as there is in the High Court: 

 "... an inherent jurisdiction to restrain the institution of proceedings by named persons in order to ensure that the process of the court is not abused by repeated attempts to reopen litigation or to pursue litigation which is plainly groundless and vexatious. The court is bound to uphold the rights of other citizens, including their right to be protected from unnecessary harassment and expense, rights which are enjoyed by the holders of public offices as well as by private citizens. This court would be failing in its duty, as would the High Court, if it allowed its processes to be repeatedly invoked in order to reopen issues already determined or to pursue groundless and vexatious litigation." 

 128.           The case of S.P. v. U.G. [2016] IEHC 693 , in which Abbott J. made Isaac Wunder orders, was also referred to where it was noted at para. 22 as follows: 

 "The source of such power to make an Isaac Wunder order comes from the implied power that arises from the duty of all courts to supervise and control their own procedures so as not to be oppressive or to allow parties to be endlessly subject to vexatious applications and litigating [sic] being repeatedly brought before the courts." 

 129.           Reference was also made by the Attorney General to a number of other cases in which the making of such orders was required to prevent misuse of the court process. In that context, reference was made to the decisions in O'Connor v. Property Registration Authority of Ireland [2024] IECA 264 , Bula Limited (In Receivership) v. Crowley & Others [2009] IESC 35 , Talbot v. Hermitage Golf Club & Ors [2014] IESC 57 , and Heuston v. Doyle [2020] IECA 289 . As emphasised in the submissions of the Attorney General, serial, abusive, or vexatious conduct of litigation engages two important but distinct interests: namely, the private interest of a party in not being subject to such litigation, and the public interest in ensuring that the courts' time and attention is not manifestly distorted by such litigation. Commenting on these different interests, it was observed on behalf of the Attorney General that the protection of the public interest may, in an appropriate case, require greater flexibility in the kinds of orders considered and, potentially, in the extent of any restriction on an individual's entitlement to engage with the court system. 

 130.           The submissions of the Attorney General then examined the position under the law of England and Wales, and in this context referred to the decision in Grepe v. Loam , referred to previously. Reference was also made to the provision contained in s. 42 of the Senior Courts Act 1981. The Attorney General also referred to the decision in Bhamjee v. Forsdick (No. 2), which is referred to above in detail. In particular, emphasis was placed by the Attorney General on two passages from Bhamjee , in which the Court of Appeal observed at para. 15 as follows: 

 "A court's overriding objective is to deal with cases justly. This means, among other things, dealing with cases expeditiously and allotting to them an appropriate share of its resources (while taking into account the need to allot resources to other cases). This objective is thwarted and the process of the court abused if litigants bombard the court with hopeless applications. They thereby divert the court's resources from dealing with meritorious disputes, delay the handling of those disputes, and waste skilled and scarce resources on matters totally devoid of any merit." 

 131.           The Attorney General also referred to the concluding remarks of the Court in Bhamjee , at para. 33, where it was said as follows: 

 "It is therefore well established on authority that: 

 (i)        This court, like any court, has an inherent jurisdiction to protect its process from abuse; 

 (ii)       The categories of abuse of process will never be closed; 

 (iii)      No litigant has any substantive right to trouble the court with litigation which represents an abuse of its process; 

 (iv)       So long as the very essence of a litigant's right to access the court is not extinguished a court has a right to regulate its processes as it thinks fit (absent any statute or rule or practice direction to contrary effect) so long as its remedies are proportionate to the identified abuse (whether it is existing or threatened); 

 (v)        One way in which a court may legitimately regulate its processes is by prescribing a procedure to be conducted entirely in writing." 

 132.           The approach commended in the case of Bhamjee was reflected in the subsequent decision in AG v. Ebert [2002] 2 All ER 789 , in which wide-ranging orders were made on the Attorney General's application for an injunction in that case. It was said therein by Brook L.J., at para. 35, as follows: 

 "We accept Mr. Keith's submission that the court's supervisory role now extends beyond the mere regulation of litigation and of litigants who have submitted themselves to the compulsory jurisdiction of the court. It includes the regulation of the manner in which the court process may in general be utilised. ... The advent of the CPR only serves to bolster the principle that in the exercise of its inherent jurisdiction the court has the power to restrain litigants from wasting the time of court staff and disturbing the orderly conduct of court processes in a completely excessive pursuit of their own litigation, taking it forward by one unmeritorious application after another and insisting that they should be afforded priority over other litigants". 

 133.           Having referred to a Practice Direction introduced in the U.K. providing for limited civil restraint orders, extended civil restraint orders, and general civil restraint orders (see Practice Direction 3C, which supplements rule 3.11 of the Civil Procedure Rules), the observation was made on behalf of the Attorney General that, while there have been a number of procedures introduced in that jurisdiction, the courts there have n­­ot confined themselves to the making of orders in accordance with s. 42 of the Senior Courts Act 1981, or indeed the Practice Direction. In other words, despite the considerable regulation of steps designed to stop vexatious litigation that amounts to abuse of process, the courts there have continued to develop steps to prevent such abuse, relying on the inherent powers of the court. 

 Some Conclusions 

 134.           There are some conclusions that can be drawn from the discussion above. It is clear that the courts have a wide variety of procedures that can be followed and orders that can be made to prevent and stop litigation that is vexatious or an abuse of the process of the courts. Such litigation obviously has an adverse effect on the opposing party, but just as importantly, it has an adverse effect on the administration of justice by wasting valuable court time on unmeritorious litigation. The remedies available to the courts include the striking out of vexatious pleadings, the striking out of abusive proceedings, and, of course, the making of Isaac Wunder orders where there is repeated unmeritorious litigation by a party to proceedings. 

 135.           An Isaac Wunder order is to be made sparingly. Access to justice is an important constitutional right but nevertheless, in an appropriate case, there may be some restrictions on the right of access to the courts. Accordingly, an Isaac Wunder order will only be made after a number of unmeritorious applications have been made by the party concerned. The making of such an order does not preclude a party from enjoying their right of access to justice, given that the sole effect of such an order is to restrict such party from initiating a new application or proceedings without the leave of the court. As such, if the party concerned is in a position to establish grounds for bringing a further application, or issuing further proceedings, then that will be permitted. It must be borne in mind that an Isaac Wunder order is not made as a matter of routine. It is simply the requirement of a party to obtain leave of the Court (usually the President of the Court or a judge nominated by the President) before instituting fresh proceedings or application against a specific defendant. It is not a restriction on the issuing of proceedings in a statable case. If the case is unstateable, for example, because the points raised have already been considered and determined in earlier proceedings, leave will not be granted. There is nothing unusual about requiring a party to obtain leave of the court for certain types of proceedings such as most types of judicial review. It is a further procedural step that must be taken but that is as far as it goes. What has to be established before leave will be granted will be discussed below. 

 136.           There is no bar to making an Isaac Wunder order in family law proceedings. This was accepted on behalf of the appellant, and it has to be said, it would be somewhat surprising if any other view was expressed by the appellant, given that the suggestion of making such an order in these proceedings came from the appellant himself as an alternative to making an order for costs, as set out above. 

 137.           Family law proceedings can be, by their nature, the subject of multiple applications to the court, because certain orders made in such proceedings are not " final " orders, in the sense that orders in other types of proceedings can be said to be. For example, issues relating to maintenance can be re-opened where there has been a change of circumstances of one or other of the parties to such proceedings. Over the course of time, it would be surprising if certain types of orders in such proceedings did not have to be revisited. 

 138.           In the case of family law proceedings, the best interests of the child have to be taken into account before making an Isaac Wunder order concerning matters such as applications in relation to custody, access, or maintenance. There may be other areas of family law proceedings that also require the best interests of the child to be taken into account - this is not intended to be an exhaustive list of the areas in which these interests have to be considered. 

 139.           It should be borne in mind that in many cases, a child, while not a party to the proceedings, may be adversely affected by a constant series of applications, for example, in relation to custody/access. Repetitious applications which are unmeritorious will inevitably have the effect of causing increased disharmony and acrimony within the family setting, and have the potential to cause other problems, such as the expenditure of large sums of money on costs which would be better spent on the family as a whole. In particular, in the context of custody/access proceedings, the child may be required to undergo repeated psychological or similar assessments for the purpose of the proceedings. This is unlikely to be beneficial to the child. 

 140.           In considering whether to make an Isaac Wunder order, a court must act proportionately. 

 141.           The structured approach to the making of such orders advocated for on behalf of the appellant is something that could be considered by the legislature, and/or the Rules Committees of the courts, but there is nothing to suggest that the manner in which such orders now fall to be made gives rise to uncertainty or lack of clarity or proportionality as was suggested. Such orders are made in accordance with well-established case law. While from time to time, Rules of court are amended to reflect such well-established case law, as, for example, in the case of the recent amendment to O. 19, r. 28 of the RSC, the fact that no such change has been introduced for the making of Isaac Wunder orders does not present a difficulty to the making of such orders. The introduction of Rules or indeed Practice Directions to deal with such applications may be of assistance but, as of now, no specific problem has been shown to exist which would preclude the making of such orders. 

 142.           Finally, it should be observed that the making of such orders, being part of the inherent powers of the court to prevent an abuse of process, may not be confined to the High Court, the Court of Appeal, and the Supreme Court. Further, in principle, it appears that such orders can be made by the Circuit Court and the District Court despite some judicial pronouncements to the contrary but subject to certain limitations which are about to be discussed. 

 Courts of Local and Limited Jurisdiction 

 143.           The Circuit Court and District Court are courts of local and limited jurisdiction with a right of appeal as determined by law (see Article 34.3.4 ° of the Constitution). The precise extent of what is meant by "local and limited" need not be determined in these proceedings but, as Clarke C. J. observed in Permanent TSB v Langan [2018] 1 IR 375, the requirements of Article 34.3.4 must nonetheless be respected. Thus, assuming that these courts have jurisdiction to make Isaac Wunder orders, it would appear that some geographical or other limitation must necessarily apply in relation to the jurisdiction or venue in relation to which such orders may be made. Of course, the extent of the jurisdiction of the Circuit Court to make such orders gave rise to an issue in these proceedings. The order made in the Circuit Court herein precluded the appellant from taking any further proceedings in the District Court, Circuit Court, or, for that matter, any other court, without leave of the Circuit Court. As Simons J. said at para. 16 of his judgment herein: 

 "It is unnecessary, for the purpose of resolving the procedural objection raised in the present case, to determine whether the Circuit Court possesses its own independent jurisdiction to make a restraining order in respect of proceedings before it. Whatever the precise position may be in this regard, the Circuit Court most certainly does not have jurisdiction to impose a restriction in the right of access to the High Court. The High Court exercises a supervisory jurisdiction over the Circuit Court, by way of judicial review, and the Circuit Court cannot frustrate the exercise of that supervisory jurisdiction by purporting to oblige a party to obtain prior permission from the Circuit Court before having recourse to the High Court. If and insofar as the order of 23 May 2022 purports to impose such an obligation - and it is not apparent from the transcript that this is what the Circuit Court judge actually intended - this represents an error on the face of the record. This aspect of the order cannot oust the High Court's full original jurisdiction to entertain these judicial review proceedings." 

 144.           For the avoidance of doubt, I should add that as part of its supervisory role in relation to both the Circuit Court and the District Court, I see no reason why the High Court could not, in an appropriate case make an Isaac Wunder order in respect of proceedings in the Circuit Court and the District Court. Further, it seems to me that in an appropriate case, the High Court must have jurisdiction to injunct a party from commencing or continuing proceedings in the Circuit or District Court where those proceedings would amount to an abuse of process   Leaving aside the question of Isaac Wunder orders, it appears that the High Court apart from its supervisory role over the Circuit and Districts courts by means of judicial review has had a longstanding supervisory role in relation to some aspects case of contempt of court whereby the High Court has jurisdiction to punish parties for contempt of court occurring in the District and Circuit Court. This simply reflects the long-standing supervisory role of the High Court in respect of those courts. (For an interesting discussion on this issue, see the LRC Consultation Paper on Contempt (p.p. 182-184 and the cases of Attorney General v O'Ryan and Boyd [1947] IR 213 and AG v Connolly [1946] IR 82.) I have read the judgment of Murray J. where he deals with the supervisory role of the High Court and I agree with the views expressed therein. 

 145.           The Court of Appeal in its judgment in this matter did not deal with this aspect of the proceedings in any detail, saying simply at para. 6 of the second judgment as follows: 

 "The issue which then arose was whether that small outstanding balance of these proceedings (regarding the validity of the Isaac Wunder order made by the Circuit Court) should be remitted to the High Court for determination, in circumstances where the trial judge had cast doubt upon the validity of that order as made, and where remittal would, inevitably, give rise to further costs. The Court indicated to the parties that, in the alternative, this Court could make an order quashing the Isaac Wunder order and proceed to entertain an application by the applicant for a fresh Isaac Wunder order. The parties agreed to this course of action, and subsequently written submissions were filed and a supplemental hearing was held on this issue." 

 146.           It seems to me that the reasoning employed by Simons J. in para. 16 of his judgment set out above is correct. He was of the view that the Circuit Court does not have jurisdiction to make an order ousting the jurisdiction of the High Court, which has full original jurisdiction. That must be so and does not require further elaboration. 

 147.           That does not answer the question of whether the Circuit Court (and the District Court) has itself jurisdiction to make such orders. Overall, it appears to me that in circumstances where the making of an Isaac Wunder order is part of a court's panoply of powers to protect the administration of justice from an abuse of process, it would be difficult to see why the Circuit Court could not make such orders, if necessary and appropriate in the circumstances. Dealing with the jurisdiction of the Circuit Court, it will be noted that the Courts (Supplemental Provisions) Act 1961 ("the 1961 Act") and, in particular, s. 22(1)(a) provides: 

 " Subject to paragraphs (b) and (c) of this subsection, the Circuit Court shall, concurrently with the High Court, have all the jurisdiction of the High Court to hear and determine any proceedings of the kind mentioned in column (2) of the Third Schedule to this Act at any reference number ." 

 148.           While this section concerns the type of proceedings which can be heard by the Circuit Court (subject to quantitative limits), it is noteworthy that the Circuit Court has " all the jurisdiction of the High Court " to deal with such proceedings. It would also be worth mentioning the provisions of s. 22(6) of the 1961 Act. It provides as follows: 

 "The Circuit Court, as regards any cause of action for the time being within its jurisdiction , shall, in any proceedings before it- 

 (a)    Grant such relief, redress or remedy or combination of remedies, absolute or conditional, 

 (b)    Give such and the like effect to every round of defence or counterclaim, legal or equitable, 

 as ought to be granted or given in the like case by the High Court and in as full and ample a manner." 

 These specific provisions may lead to the view that,  bearing in mind that the High Court has jurisdiction to make such orders, it follows from the terms of s.22 (6) of the 1961 Act that the Circuit Court must also have the same jurisdiction and power to make an Isaac Wunder order, subject to any limits relating to the local and limited nature of the jurisdiction of the Circuit Court. While these are  important provisions in relation to the overall jurisdiction of the Circuit Court and  the manner in which it exercises its jurisdiction, I am satisfied that the Circuit Court, as a court established under the Constitution to administer the law, has an inherent power to make Isaac Wunder orders in order to protest the administration of justice  and is not reliant on the provisions of s. 22 (6) to do so. 

 149.           This is so notwithstanding the decision of the Court of Appeal in the case of Morgan v. The Labour Court & Ors [2025] IECA 2 referred to by the appellant. That was a case in which Isaac Wunder orders were made by the High Court following the hearing of a number of applications including appeals from the Labour Court. In the course of the hearing before the High Court, it was noted that the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) had a statutory power to strike out proceedings that were " frivolous or vexatious " but it had no jurisdiction to make an Isaac Wunder- type order . Whelan J., giving the judgment of the Court of Appeal, commented at para. 172 of her judgment: 

 "The WRC and the Labour Court, as creatures of statute, lack any inherent jurisdiction. The ambit of their respective powers is delineated by the relevant governing legislation." 

 150.           The issue at the heart of that case was the jurisdiction of the High Court to extend the ambit of the Isaac Wunder orders to cover proceedings before the WRC and the Labour Court, and it was concluded therein that there was such jurisdiction. 

 151.           The point was made therein that the power of those bodies, as creatures of statute, was delineated by the relevant governing legislation. That is undoubtedly so. The Circuit Court is also a creature of statute, albeit provided for by the Constitution as previously mentioned. However, having been established, it is a Court established under the Constitution engaged in the administration of justice. In the case of the Circuit Court, as I have explained above, the jurisdiction of the Circuit Court is sufficiently wide, in my view, to enable that Court to make Isaac Wunder orders  by reason of its inherent power.. It is not subject to the limitations applicable to the WRC and the Labour Court which are not courts established under the Constitution and whose jurisdiction is limited by statute to striking out frivolous or vexatious litigation. 

 152.           While the jurisdiction conferred on the District Court by the 1961 Act is set out in different terms and not expressed as being co-extensive with that of the High Court in the way that the Circuit Court is expressly stated to be (see s. 33 of the 1961 Act),  the Attorney General, in response to questions raised by the Court in this regard, made the point that the District and Circuit Courts are obliged to administer justice in compliance with the Constitution and such obligation is not affected by those courts being of local and limited jurisdiction. Reference was made to the decision in the case of The People v. Lynch [1982] I.R. 64 (at p. 84) where Walsh J explained: 

 "...the judges of the District Court and judges of the Circuit Court are not dispensed from, or expected to overlook, their constitutional obligation to uphold the constitution in the discharge of their constitutional and legal function of administering justice." 

 153.           Reference was also made to the comments of Geoghegan J. in Whelan v. Kirby [2004] IESC 17 , [2005] 2 IR 30 in which he observed: 

 "There is jurisdiction in the District Court to make any order that would be necessary for the fulfilment of the constitutional obligation of a fair trial and fair procedures." 

 154.           Thus, while the terms of the legislation conferring jurisdiction on the Circuit Court and the District Court are expressed differently, both courts are engaged in the process of the administration of justice. The jurisdiction of the District Court is less extensive than the Circuit Court, but nonetheless, it seems to me that the District Court, no less than any other Court, is entitled to ensure that proceedings before it are not used in such a way as to amount to an abuse of process. To refer back to the earlier discussion on inherent powers and inherent jurisdiction, it seems to me that every court has the power to regulate the proceedings before it, and this includes restricting proceedings which amount to an abuse of process. It would seem strange if the District Court was powerless in the face of an abuse of process to take any steps to prevent such abuse. The passages referred to from the Lynch case and Whelan v. Kirby above make it clear that both the Circuit Court and the District Court have obligations under the Constitution in relation to fair trials and fair procedures when engaged in the administration of justice. That obligation must include the possibility of restricting access to court when the proceedings constitute an abuse of process. In the circumstances, it seems to me that the powers of the District Court in exercising its jurisdiction encompass the inherent power of a court to make orders which are necessary to prevent an abuse of process. Thus, while I have referred above to the statutory provisions in relation to the jurisdiction of the Circuit Court, it seems to me that the important basis for the making of such orders  is the inherent power of a court engaged in the administration of justice to make an Isaac Wunder order when the administration of justice so requires. Accordingly, regardless of the differences in the terms of the legislation setting out the respective jurisdictions of the Circuit and District Court, both courts must have the same inherent power to make such orders as are necessary to ensure that the administration of justice in those courts is protected from abuse. 

 155.           It could, however, be argued that there is an issue as to the geographical limit of orders of the Circuit Court. In other words, can an order made by a Circuit judge sitting in the Dublin Circuit, for example, preclude an application being made to issue proceedings in another circuit of the Circuit Court? There is an interesting discussion of the local and limited jurisdiction of the Circuit Court to be found in the case of Permanent TSB plc v Langan [2017] IESC 71 , [2018] 1 I.R. 375 in which Clarke CJ observed: 

 "67. The requirement that the court be "local" clearly causes no difficulties in cases such as this for the property jurisdiction of the Circuit Court is ordinarily conferred on the circuit in which the property concerned is situated. The issue which arose for debate was, however concerned with the requirement that the jurisdiction be "limited". On that basis it was said that the court might be required, in order that the interpretation to be placed on the legislation was consistent with the Constitution, to refrain from adopting an interpretation which would confer an unlimited jurisdiction on the Circuit Court in cases such as this." 

 He went on to say: 

 " 74. A real meaning must be given to the requirement that the jurisdiction of a court such as the Circuit Court is limited. To do otherwise would be to disregard the Constitution. But it is not necessary to go so far as to require that each and every category of case in which a jurisdiction is conferred on the Circuit Court must have a monetary or value limitation. However, that being said, it might be the case that to confer a jurisdiction in a very wide category of case without any limitation might cause constitutional difficulties." 

 The observations of Clarke C.J. in that case focussed principally on the nature of the "limited" jurisdiction of the Circuit Court but while that was the principal issue, his observations on the "local" jurisdiction are of importance. As he noted in that case, jurisdiction is " ordinarily conferred on the circuit in which the property concerned is situated". Just as it is the case that the jurisdiction of the Circuit Court is ordinarily restricted in property disputes to the area in which the property is situated, there are also limitations on where proceedings can be brought in family law proceedings. In this context, Order 59 of the Rules of the Circuit Court provides for the venue for such proceedings, in the county where the applicant or a child to whom the application relates ordinarily resides. There is also provision for proceedings to be brought where the applicant carries on any profession, business or occupation. Thus, the Circuit Court is not at large in terms of the location in which it exercises its jurisdiction. I am conscious of the fact that a party commencing proceedings in the Circuit Court may, on the facts of a particular case, have a choice of venue. It could, for example, be where the other party resides or works. In some cases the choice of venue may be restricted, for example, in proceedings relating to property. This view applies also to the jurisdiction of the District Court. It is limited as to venue in making orders by reference to the relevant District Court's particular functional area. Thus, it follows that  an order made by the Circuit Court could not be enforced other than in a Circuit in which the particular Circuit is the appropriate venue for any necessary proceedings, as determined by the Rules of the Circuit Court. It is important not to overstate the geographical limitations on the jurisdictions of the Circuit and District Courts. An order of each of those Courts is of validity regardless of where it has been made but it's enforceability by courts in other Circuits or Districts is limited by reference to the Rules of those Courts as to venue. For example, a judgment of the Dublin Circuit Court for damages in a personal injuries action is not a judgment which is valid only in Dublin. It can be enforced elsewhere in the country, provided that the place in which it is sought to enforced is a place which has jurisdiction to enforce it, because, for example,  the judgment debtor has property there. Thus, an Isaac Wunder order, whether made by the District Court or the Circuit Court is of validity throughout the country as a whole and restricts the person bound by such an order from issuing fresh proceedings elsewhere in the country. I appreciate the fact that Collins J. in a judgment which he is about to deliver herein takes a different view on this question (see para 18 et seq. thereof) but for my part, I do not take the view that the essence of the local and limited jurisdiction of the Circuit Court or, indeed, the District Court, is such that an order made in one Circuit or District cannot have legal effect outside the boundaries of that Circuit or District. It is important to bear in  mind that an Isaac Wunder  order made against an individual litigant in respect of litigation involving the same party in respect of the same type of litigation is effective regardless of the Circuit or District in which it was made. However, it is important to remember the limits of the jurisdiction of those courts. A party can only initiate proceedings in a venue which has jurisdiction to deal with the matter, Thus, an  Isaac Wunder order will only be effective in a Circuit or District in which the relevant Court would otherwise have jurisdiction to deal with the matter.  This is because the nature of such an order is that it is an order in personam  and is limited to the parties in the relevant litigation. An Isaac Wunder order should reflect these limitations and should not be formulated by the Circuit or District Court in such a way as to preclude the party the subject of the order from litigating against other parties not involved in the subject litigation or in respect of other issues which are unrelated to the subject matter of the litigation affected by the order. That is not to suggest that the High Court in the exercise of its full and original jurisdiction cannot make more extensive orders where appropriate. Accordingly, I agree with the views expressed by Murray J. in the judgment he is about to deliver on this issue. For completeness, I should add that I agree with the views of Hogan J. on this issue as set out in his judgment herein. 

 156.           Finally, reference should also be made to Grimes v Owners of SS Bangor Bay [1948] I.R. 350, an admiralty action, in which O'Byrne J. considered Article 34.3.4° by referring back to Article 64 of the Constitution of 1922, part of which was in similar terms, saying at p. 358: 

 "that it enjoine[d] and require[d] that [the Circuit Court] should be local and limited in its jurisdiction.. [Though one Court] its jurisdiction is to be exercised locally by the judges of that court in the manner specified by s.52 and this section was intended, in my opinion, to satisfy the constitutional requirement that the jurisdiction of courts of first instance, other than the High Court, should be local...If a statute purported to confer upon any court of first instance, other than the High Court, such unlimited jurisdiction, it would, in my opinion, contravene the clear intendment of the Constitution." 

 157.              While there may be possibly be a difference in emphasis between what was said by O'Byrne J. in Grimes and the subsequent comments of Clarke C.J. in Langan, the key point which emerges from both decisions is that the local and limited requirement simply requires that the jurisdiction of the District Court and the Circuit Court must be rooted by reference to venue. The interpretation of this is, however, largely a matter for the Oireachtas: Article 34.3.4⁰ is largely accommodating in nature rather than being prescriptive in character. While neither the District Court or the Circuit Court can be invested with what amounts to the High Court's full original jurisdiction, then in Casey's words ("The Constitution and the Legal System" (1979) 14 Irish Jurist 1 at 14): 

 "Short of this, the extent and amplitude of jurisdiction conferred on the lower courts would seem to be a matter within the discretion of the Oireachtas. The Constitution, as the framework for government in a changing society, must surely be interpreted to afford the flexibility which social and economic developments may require. Restrictions on the jurisdiction of the Circuit Court thought appropriate twenty years ago may no longer be suitable; and in so far as they depend on the absence of appropriate machinery in that court, the remedy is plainly in the hands of Government and the Oireachtas." 

 I consider that this passage neatly summarises the effect of the local and limited requirements contained in Article 34.3.4.⁰ 

 158.              Finally, as observed previously, I am satisfied that the Circuit Court cannot make an order restricting the issue of proceedings in the High Court. Equally, I cannot see any basis for the District Court to make any order restricting the issue of proceedings in the Circuit Court. It must be borne in mind that the power of the courts to make these types of orders is to protect such courts from an abuse of process before the relevant court. I am fortified in this view by the express words of  s. 22 (6) of the 1961 Act set out above which provides that the Circuit  Court has jurisdiction "as regards any cause of action for the time being within its jurisdiction " (my emphasis). 

 159.              Given the clear limits on the exercise of such power, it follows that the limited jurisdiction of both the District Court and the Circuit Court could not be such as to enable such Courts to make orders restricting the issue of proceedings in Courts which enjoy a greater jurisdiction under the Constitution. 

 

 The Court of Appeal Order: Discussion 

 160.              A number of points were made by the appellant in arguing that the Court of Appeal erred in making an Isaac Wunder order in this case. First of all, reference was made to the fact that less intrusive measures were not considered which might have the same effect as an Isaac Wunde r order, while respecting the appellant's rights and the best interests of the child. It was submitted that the making of an Isaac Wunder order did not accord with the principle of proportionality. It was also said that the Court of Appeal failed to have regard to the best interests of the child. Further, it was argued that the Court of Appeal failed to have regard to the dynamic nature of family law disputes. It was then suggested that the Court of Appeal should have considered making an order that was time-limited, or specific issue-related, rather than a blanket prohibition on issuing proceedings or applications. In these circumstances, it was said that the Isaac Wunder order made herein was disproportionate and unduly restrictive. 

 161.              For her part, the respondent took issue with the contention that the making of an Isaac Wunder order was disproportionate. She pointed out that such orders are only made in exceptional cases, upon proof of the type of exceptional circumstances that are required to enable the making of such order. She takes issue with the arguments that there was any error on the part of the Court of Appeal in making that order. She made the point that the Court of Appeal in this case would have been in error had it not made an Isaac Wunder order, and went on to point out that a failure to make such an order in a case of this kind would have the effect of depriving the respondent of an important remedy, in circumstances where she had been subjected to unduly protracted, oppressive, vexatious, and unnecessarily costly family litigation. 

 162.              In order to consider this issue properly, it is necessary to look at the judgment of the Court of Appeal of the 28 th June, 2024, in which it opted to make an Isaac Wunder order. In that regard, the Court of Appeal had regard to the decision in the case of Riordan v. Ireland (No. 4) , the case of M.M. v. G.M. , S.P. v. U.G. , all referred to above previously, and, finally, Burke v. Judge Fulham [2010] IEHC 448 . Woulfe J. set out the principles identified by Irvine J. (as she then was) in the Burke case, set out at para. 12 above. 

 163.              Having observed that he agreed with the approach set out by Irvine J. in Burke , Woulfe J. added that: 

 "... the above factors should be looked at in a broad untechnical way, as a list of potential factors capable of adaptation and extension, rather than in any literal or mechanical way, having regard to the broad nature of the jurisdiction described by this Court in Riordan (No. 4)." 

 164.              He then applied the legal principles set out in Burke to the facts of this case (see paras. 13 - 15 above). While the appellant complained that the Court of Appeal in its judgment did not have regard to the best interests of the child, I think this is, to some extent, a mischaracterisation of the way in which the Court of Appeal dealt with the matter. The Court of Appeal had regard to three uncontested affidavits sworn by the respondent herein setting out the actions of the appellant. The Court clearly had regard to all of the facts and circumstances in the case. That included the fact that the nature of the litigation was causing " significant stress and anxiety on the part of the minor child " (judgment, para. 8). 

 165.              For my part, I am satisfied that the Court of Appeal did not err in making the Isaac Wunder order, having regard to the facts and circumstances of this case. The respondent herein has been subjected to a barrage of unmeritorious litigation. As Woulfe J. said at para. 30: 

 "... a situation has been reached where to permit the [appellant] an unrestricted right to continue to litigate against the respondent would be unfair and oppressive to the respondent, and a waste of scarce court time and resources to the detriment of other litigants." 

 166.              This litigation has occurred at a great cost to the respondent, both in terms of stress and anxiety and in financial terms. Restricting such litigation by way of an Isaac Wunder is an entirely appropriate response to the behaviour of the appellant. 

 167.              While the appellant urged this Court to adopt a less restrictive approach in the circumstances of this type of litigation in particular, involving a family dispute, I see no merit in that suggestion. While an Isaac Wunder order restricts a litigant from issuing new proceedings or applications, it is a restriction which can be lifted by prior leave of the President of the court concerned. In a case in which it is appropriate to grant leave, that will be done. There is no reason why any application for leave could not be dealt with expeditiously. Accordingly, there is no basis for overturning the decision of the Court of Appeal in this regard. 

 General Powers of  the Court when presented with Serial Litigants: Discussion 

 168.              The appellant in dealing with this issue referred to the fact that the courts have a range of powers at their disposal to safeguard the administration of justice.
