However, it was reiterated that any restriction on the right of access to the courts had to be proportionate, respect the principle of legal certainty, and uphold a litigant's fundamental rights under both the Constitution and the Convention. 

 169.              It was argued that the principle of proportionality requires that any restriction imposed is the least restrictive measure necessary to achieve the legitimate aim of preventing abuse. Reference was made to the decision in Brumarescu v. Romania (App. No. 28342/95) [1999] VII E.H.R.R. 862, in which the European Court of Human Rights, referring to Article 6.1 of the Convention, pointed out that: 

 "One of the fundamental aspects of the rule of law is the principle of legal certainty, ..." 

 170.              It was suggested on behalf of the appellant that the current approach to the making of Isaac Wunder orders does not fully accord with the principle of legal certainty and, once more, the appellant urged on this Court that a model such as that employed in the courts of England and Wales, referred to above, was a more structured and transparent framework within which to deal with vexatious litigants. Accordingly, it was submitted that a more calibrated approach to restraining orders should be adopted in this jurisdiction. 

 171.              For her part, the respondent referred to a number of powers of the courts, such as the power to strike out or dismiss proceedings, the power in relation to the making of costs orders or requiring security for costs, the use of case management to discourage delay, and the jurisdiction of the courts in relation to contempt. Reference was also made to the power of a court to strike out proceedings under O. 19, r. 28 of the RSC. It was pointed out that, in circumstances where it was necessary to clarify or correct a misrepresentation about prior proceedings, a transcript of the proceedings could be obtained, and that would include, in appropriate cases, the digital audio recording of previous proceedings. However, the point was made that none of the remedies available in ordinary civil litigation could address misconduct in the context of family law litigation, because of the fact that principles such as res judicata , issue estoppel, and the rule in Henderson v. Henderson (1843) 3 Hare 100 , 67 ER 313 were not readily applicable to some issues in family law proceedings. As I pointed out previously, certain family law orders cannot be regarded as 'final' in the way that a final order is understood in relation to ordinary civil litigation. In that context, the respondent submitted an Isaac Wunder order was an appropriate remedy in such proceedings. 

 172.              She made the point that such orders can be obtained in a manner which is inherently flexible and efficient. She submitted that, as an application for leave to bring proceedings or a further application is made before the President or nominated judge who must deal with the matter constitutionally by reference to the rights of all affected parties, having regard to both the Constitution and the Convention, that it was a fluid and fair process which admits of a variety of orders shaped to the nature of the case. She argued that the absence of statutory rules in this country heightened the need to maintain the availability of Isaac Wunder orders, as it is a necessary tool to protect the courts processes and to prevent abuse by vexatious litigants. The fact that a party against whom such an order is made retains the right to obtain leave or, indeed, in an appropriate case, to apply to have the Isaac Wunder order vacated upon the showing of good reason, requires courts to adhere to the principles of justice and to balance the rights of all affected parties in a proportionate manner. 

 173.              The Attorney General in his submissions likewise referred to a number of the inherent powers of the courts, such as: 

 ·          the power to strike out proceedings as an abuse of process, or otherwise doomed to fail; 

 ·          the dismissal of proceedings where the litigant's conduct makes their continuation impossible; 

 ·          the making of an order restraining a litigant from bringing proceedings without permission against a named party, or in particular proceedings; 

 ·          the making of an order restraining a litigant from bringing proceedings without permission that relate to, or touch on, an issue previously determined in other proceedings; 

 ·          the making of an order restraining a litigant from bringing proceedings without permission in general; 

 ·          the making of orders in any of the above requiring that a litigant seek permission in writing only, and/or specified judge(s); 

 ·          the making of an order requiring that a litigant provide security for costs prior to the bringing of proceedings in any of the above situations; 

 ·          the making of an order for costs in any of the above situations that measures costs and requires that they be discharged prior to any further application being brought; 

 ·          the making of orders freezing or otherwise sequestering assets where they may be used to prevent default of the court orders above; 

 ·          the use of the contempt jurisdiction to protect the process or integrity of the court process; 

 ·          the imposition of an injunction preventing a litigant from being present in the precincts of a court building without permission; 

 ·          the imposition of an injunction preventing a litigant from seeking to address a court on their own behalf, and/or as a McKenzie friend. 

 174.              As was pointed out on behalf of the Attorney General, such powers would require to be balanced against competing considerations, including the constitutional right of access to the courts. It was acknowledged that this was an aspect of the  rights protected by Article 6 of the Convention. As was noted, the right of access to the courts is not an absolute right and may be subject to appropriate limitations. The observations of Noonan J. in the case of Leslie Fitzsimons v. Bank of Scotland Plc. & Tanager Ltd. [2019] IECA 336 were referred to, in which it was stated at para. 24 as follows: 

 "The making of an Isaac Wunder order is not an abrogation of the constitutional right of access to the court, but rather a proportionate filtering mechanism to protect the opposing party from the injustice of having to incur what are often very significant and unrecoverable costs, in meeting oppressive and abusive claims." 

 175.              Reference was also made in the submissions of the Attorney General to the case of Kearney v. Bank of Scotland Plc. [2020] IECA 92 . At para. 132, the Court of Appeal in its judgment set out a number of principles to be applied to the making of Isaac Wunder orders. It said: 

 "Isaac Wunder orders now form part of the panoply of the courts' inherent powers to regulate their own process. In light of the constitutional protection of the right of access to the courts, such orders should be deployed sparingly and only be made where a clear case has been made out that demonstrates the necessity of the making of the orders in the circumstances: 

 i.        Regard can be had by the court to the history of litigation between the parties or other parties connected with them in relation to common issues. 

 ii.       Regard can be had also to the nature of allegations advanced and in particular where scurrilous or outrageous statements are asserted including fraud against a party to litigation or their legal representatives or other professionals connected with the other party to the litigation. 

 iii.      The court ought to be satisfied that there are good grounds for believing that there will be further proceedings instituted by a claimant before an Isaac Wunder type order restraining the prosecution of litigation or the institution of fresh litigation is made. 

 iv.      Regard may be had to the issue of costs and the conduct of the litigant in question with regard to the payment and discharge of costs orders incurred up to the date of the making of the order by defendants and indeed by past defendants in applications connected with the issues the subject matter of the litigation. 

 v.       The balancing exercise between the competing rights of the parties is to be carried out with due regard to the constitutional rights of a litigant and in general no legitimate claim brought by a plaintiff ought to be precluded from being heard and determined in a court of competent jurisdiction save in exceptional circumstances. 

 vi.      It is not the function of the courts to protect a litigant from his own insatiable appetite for litigation and an Isaac Wunder type order is intended to operate preferably as an early stage compulsory filter, necessitated by the interests of the common good and the need to ensure that limited court resources are available to those who require same most and not dissipated and for the purposes of saving money and time for all parties and for the court. 

 vii.     Such orders should provide a delimitation on access to the court only to the extent necessitated in the interests of the common good. 

 viii.     Regard should be had to the fact that the right of access to the courts to determine a genuine and serious dispute about the existence of a right or interest, subject to limitations clearly defined in the jurisprudence and by statute, is constitutionally protected, was enshrined in clause 40 of Magna Carta of 1215 and is incorporated into the European Convention on Human Rights by article 6, to which the courts have regard in the administration of justice in this jurisdiction since the coming into operation of the European Convention on Human Rights Act 2003. 

 ix.      The courts should be vigilant in regard to making such orders in circumstances where a litigant is unrepresented and may not be in a position to properly articulate his interests in maintaining access to the courts. Where possible the litigant ought to be forewarned of an intended application for an Isaac Wunder type order. In the instant case it is noteworthy that the trial judge afforded the appellant the option of giving an undertaking to refrain from taking further proceedings which he declined. 

 x.       Any power which a court may have to prevent, restrain or delimit a party from commencing or pursuing legal proceedings must be regarded as exceptional. It appears that inferior courts do not have such inherent power to prevent a party from initiating or pursuing proceedings at any level. 

 xi.      An Isaac Wunder order may have serious implications for the party against whom it is made. It potentially stigmatises such a litigant by branding her or him as, in effect, "vexatious" and this may present a risk of inherent bias in the event that a fresh application is made for leave to institute proceedings in respect of the subject matter of the order or to set aside a stay granted in litigation. 

 xii.     Where a strike out order can be made or an order dismissing litigation whether as an abuse of process or pursuant to the inherent jurisdiction of the court or pursuant to the provisions of O. 19, r. 28, same is to be preferred and a clear and compelling case must be identified as to why, in addition, an Isaac Wunder type order is necessitated by the party seeking it." 

 176.              Much of what is stated in that passage requires little or no elaboration, and reflects some important considerations; firstly, the fact that the making of an Isaac Wunder order should be a last resort and is not an order which should be lightly or routinely made. Secondly, the possibility of other alternatives that might be available and meet the purpose of bringing vexatious litigation to an end could be considered. A key factor in any case is the fact that the making of an Isaac Wunder order does, in fact, restrict a person's right of access to the courts, and thus this is an important consideration for any court contemplating the making of such order, albeit, as explained above, it is a restriction which, at most, interposes an additional procedural step before the issuing of fresh proceedings, where leave will be granted in an appropriate case. 

 177.              The Attorney General went on in his submissions to say that the powers of the Court to deal with such matters, and litigation that can be described as vexatious or an abuse of process, are " inherently flexible and capable of being adapted and applied so that any order made reflects the requirements of balance and proportionality in a particular case ". That is undoubtedly the case. The Attorney General went on to make the point that the principles referred to in Kearney should not be regarded as a form of checklist, each step of which have to be complied with before an order could be made. Again, I would agree with that submission. The one point I would make is that, for reasons already explained, I do not agree with the observation at point (x) to the effect that " it appears that inferior courts do not have any such inherent power to prevent a party from initiating or pursuing proceedings at any level " save that as noted previously, I agree with Simons J.'s observation in relation to the extent of the power of the Circuit Court in this case, and that it could not make an order that would oust the jurisdiction of the High Court (see para. 16 of his judgment referred to previously herein) and is limited to making such orders within its own jurisdiction as explained above. 

 178.              Thus, in relation to the question posed by the Court in this regard, as to the powers that a court may generally exercise when presented with a serial litigant, there is no doubt but that there are a wide number of remedies available to a court to deal with such litigants. In the case of Isaac Wunder orders, it is important to remember that the making of such an order does no more than restrict a party from access to the courts without prior leave to the President of the court, or a judge nominated by the President of that court. It is not a blanket ban on somebody issuing proceedings, for example, for a period of two years. It is simply the requirement of a party to make an application for leave before embarking on fresh proceedings. Yes, it does restrict the right of access to court, but, as has been explained, it is a form of order that is the last resort in cases where parties are the subject of oppressive litigation. It is important to observe that orders such as this are not made every day by courts in this country. The circumstances in which such orders could be made will only arise in limited circumstances. The effect of not making such orders where appropriate is to cause further distress, anxiety, and oppression to parties affected by such litigation. It is also fair to say that cases of the kind in which such orders have to be made frequently involve the excessive use of court time which, as has been emphasised previously, is scarce. Thus, two interests are served by the making of such orders, namely, the interests of the individuals affected by the making of such an order, but also the requirements of the courts to ensure that their time is not unduly spent on hopeless, vexatious, and pointless litigation. 

 179.              There is one further point to note. When a court is satisfied that it is appropriate, having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case, to make an Isaac Wunder order, it should be borne in mind that the party against whom the order has been made will, in general, have a right of appeal. As was pointed out by the Attorney General in response to questions raised by the Court, an appeal against a decision of a lower court which made an Isaac Wunder order, or an appeal against a refusal of a lower court to grant leave to bring proceedings, may involve the other party to those proceedings in further litigation concerning the appeal. Restrictions on a right to appeal are problematic. In the case of Governey v. Financial Services Ombudsman [2015] IESC 38 , [2015] 2 I.R. 616, Clarke J. addressed the issue of restrictions on the right of appeal and said at pp. 623 to 624 as follows: 

 " The point which I wish to emphasise is not that there is anything inappropriate about legislation restricting or, in appropriate cases, excluding a right of appeal. Rather, the point is that where such restriction or exclusion is sought to be achieved, it should be done by clear wording ." 

 180.              Two provisions govern appeals from the District Court to the Circuit Court, and from the Circuit Court to the High Court. Thus, s. 84 of the Courts of Justice Act 1924 provides that an appeal shall lie " in all cases other than criminal cases " from any decision of the District Court to the Circuit Court. 

 181.              So far as the Circuit Court is concerned, provision is made in ss. 37 and 38 of the Courts of Justice Act 1936, providing for an appeal to the High Court from the judgment or order in any civil action or matter. The legislation clearly does not affect the right of appeal in the case of Isaac Wunder orders. Accordingly, it is the view of the Attorney General that any order made restricting a party by way of an Isaac Wunder order, or indeed refusing leave to bring further proceedings, must be appealable. I am satisfied that this is so. It follows that the making of an Isaac Wunder order is, by its very nature, an exceptional order, and will only be made when it is necessary and proportionate to do so. The making of any such order will usually be appealable (provided it is made by a court from which an appeal lies), and, finally, insofar as it is a restriction on the right of access to justice, it is subject to the possibility of leave being granted to permit further proceedings to be issued, if appropriate to grant such leave. 

 182.              One other issue was raised in this context, and it is in relation to a situation where somebody has misrepresented what occurred in court on a previous occasion. It will be recalled that these proceedings commenced by way of proceedings for judicial review on foot of an ex parte application for leave to apply for judicial review which came before Simons J. in the first instance in August 2022. Subsequently, the respondent issued a motion seeking to set aside the grant of leave. She set out the background to the matter and raised serious issues as to the information provided to the High Court on the application for judicial review. Simons J. considered the principles applicable to setting aside a grant of leave, and noted that, in circumstances of material non-disclosure on the part of an applicant, it was possible to make an order setting aside the grant of leave. In this regard, it would be helpful to refer to para. 23 of the judgment of the Court of Appeal of the 28 th February, 2024 ( [2024] IECA 45 ) , in which the following was recorded: 

 "23.     The trial judge turned next to applying these principles to the circumstances of the present case. It was apparent to him that the applicant's characterisation of the Circuit Court hearing on the 23rd May, 2022, was grossly misleading. First, it was simply untrue to say that there was no evidence before the Circuit Court in relation to the outstanding maintenance payments, in circumstances where the respondent had given sworn oral evidence to the Court on that date and specifically confirmed that there was a sum of 3,265 outstanding. Secondly, the averment that counsel for the applicant had sought to cross examine the respondent was also untrue. Thirdly, the applicant's averment that no supportive affidavit had been sworn by the respondent was incorrect as the respondent had, in fact, filed three affidavits in support of her appeal from the District Court. 

 24.       More generally, Simons J. held that the applicant had failed to disclose the convoluted history of these family law proceedings, the case having been listed for hearing before the Circuit Court on more than forty occasions, with multiple interim orders having been made. The false impression created by the applicant's verifying affidavit was that the appeal had been determined in a peremptory manner by the Circuit Court." 

 183.              As was noted by the Court of Appeal, the trial judge found that the description of the hearing before the Circuit Court, as per the statement of grounds and verifying affidavit, was grossly misleading and conveyed the false impression that the Court had acted in breach of fair procedures and the basic rules of evidence. 

 184.              The Court of Appeal went on to conclude that, with the exception in relation to the part of the case relating to the making of the Isaac Wunder order, the trial judge was justified in setting aside almost all of the grant of leave. As the Court of Appeal said " the applicant's misstatements and non-disclosure were of a serious nature, and must be deprecated by this Court ...". 

 185.              One of the questions that falls for consideration is the nature of the powers of a court when a party before it misrepresents what occurred in court on a previous occasion. In this case, the issue arose in the context of an application for judicial review. Such proceedings are initiated generally by way of ex parte application. As such, there is an obligation of utmost good faith on the part of the person initiating the application. If that requirement is not adhered to, in an appropriate case, a respondent can make an application to have the grant of leave set aside. In this case, that was done in accordance with well-established case law. 

 186.              As was noted in the Court of Appeal, the basis upon which leave was granted fell away when it became clear that there had been no denial of fair procedures by the judge in the Circuit Court when hearing the matter originally. As such, the basis for judicial review had not been met. Central to the making of the application to set aside was the affidavit of the respondent who was able to aver to the fact that what was stated by the appellant in his grounding affidavit was simply not correct and was, in fact, misleading. Thus, the High Court and the Court of Appeal were in a position to confirm that the application for judicial review should be set aside subject to the limitation in relation to the Isaac Wunder order. It is of note that, in dealing with this matter, the High Court had the benefit of a transcript of the hearing before the Circuit Court. Although it is not stated to be the case, I presume that the transcript of the Circuit Court hearing was obtained by reference to the digital audio recording (DAR) when the application for leave to apply for judicial review was made (see para. 6 of the judgment of Simons J.). It would be unusual for the parties to have arranged for a stenographer to record the evidence in Circuit Court family law proceedings and, therefore it is likely that this was done by the production of the DAR. 

 187.              As stated above, the courts have the power to set aside an application for leave to apply for judicial review brought on a basis which is factually misleading, or as it was in this case, " grossly misleading ". That in itself is sufficient to deal with a situation such as that which occurred in this case. It is also important to note that, as a matter of practice, digital audio recording takes place in virtually every court throughout the country. It is an important safeguard for the parties before the court and, more importantly, for the courts themselves, to ensure that what occurs in court is not subsequently misrepresented. One would hope that it is not necessary on a regular basis to be required to have recourse to the DAR to actually ascertain what occurred in a particular court in the face of allegations as to what was said to have happened, or not, as the case may be. In any event, the availability of the DAR is an important safeguard to ensure the integrity of court proceedings. Accordingly, in a case where allegations of the kind that occurred in this case arise, there will be some sense of security in knowing that there is available, if needed, a record of what transpired in court. That is the most fundamental protection in relation to parties who misrepresent what occurred in court. 

 Application for leave to bring further proceedings notwithstanding the making of an Isaac Wunder order 

 188.              As was noted in the submissions of the Attorney General, the decision in Riordan v. Ireland (No. 5) [2001] 4 I.R. 463 sets out the basis upon which an application for leave to issue further proceedings can be made. In that case, Ó Caoimh J. set out the test for obtaining leave (p. 465): 

 "Where the court is satisfied that a person has habitually or persistently instituted vexatious or frivolous civil proceedings it may make an order restraining the institution of further proceedings against parties to those earlier proceedings without prior leave of the court. In assessment of the question whether the proceedings are vexatious the court is entitled to look at the whole history of the matter and it is not confined to a consideration as to whether the pleadings disclose a cause of action. The court is entitled in the assessment of whether proceedings are vexatious to consider whether they have been brought without any reasonable ground. The court has to determine whether the proceedings being brought are being brought without any reasonable ground or have been brought habitually and persistently without reasonable ground." 

 189.              In the course of that case, Ó Caoimh J. referred to a Canadian case Re Lang Michener and Fabian (1987) 37 D.L.R. (4th) 685 at p. 691, in which the following matters were set out as tending to show that a proceeding is vexatious: 

 "(a)     the bringing up on one or more actions to determine an issue which has already been determined by a court of competent jurisdiction; 

 (b)       where it is obvious that an action cannot succeed, or if the action would lead to no possible good, or if no reasonable person can reasonably expect to obtain relief; 

 (c)        where the action is brought for an improper purpose, including the harassment and oppression of other parties by multifarious proceedings brought for purposes other than the assertion of legitimate rights; 

 (d)       where issues tend to be rolled forward into subsequent actions and repeated and supplemented, often with actions brought against the lawyers who have acted for or against the litigant in earlier proceedings; 

 (e)        where the person instituting the proceedings has failed to pay the cost of unsuccessful proceedings; 

 (f)        where the respondent persistently takes unsuccessful appeals from judicial decisions." 

 190.              The comment was made by Cooke J. in the case of Kenny v. An Bord Pleanála [2010] IEHC 321 , to the effect that a court ought not to grant leave by way of exception to an Isaac Wunder order: 

 "... unless it is satisfied that the claim proposed to be served is not a vexatious repetition of the same grievance already disposed of and that it is not a claim which is manifestly unfounded or unstateable." 

 191.              Similar views were expressed by Peart J. in Daire v. The Wise Finance Company Ltd. [2018] IECA 126 at para. 18. Accordingly, it was submitted on behalf of the Attorney General that a court granting leave to bring proceedings should be satisfied: 

 1.       That the legal claim being advanced is not a repetition of previous claims or grievances on the part of the applicant, which claims have been the subject of final determination(s) by the courts; 

 2.       The legal claim being advanced is an arguable one which the applicant has a demonstrable interest in litigating. 

 192.              For his part, the appellant also referred to the decision in Riordan (No. 5) , and emphasised the fact that the test to be applied is an objective test and must balance the right of access to the courts with the need to prevent abuse of the judicial process. I have no difficulty with that contention. The respondent made the point that, when determining whether or not to grant leave, the court will necessarily consider the reasons being offered for the further litigation by reference to the previous proceedings brought by the applicant and the context in which the Isaac Wunder order was granted in the case. Where arguable grounds are shown in a bona fide manner by such an applicant, then the jurisprudence outlined above requires the court to grant the requested leave. Equally, that seems to me to be uncontroversial. 

 193.              It is abundantly clear that, in considering any such application, a court will, of necessity, have to consider the history of the previous litigation between the applicant requesting leave and the person or persons in whose favour the Isaac Wunder order was made. If legitimate grounds for bringing proceedings are established then, provided that there is an arguable claim to be brought and the applicant for leave has a proper interest in litigating the issue, leave should be granted. For my part, I am satisfied that the test for leave as articulated in the cases referred to above does not need to be adjusted.  It is important to emphasise that on any such application for leave, it will be important to have regard to the proceedings which have already taken place and the reasons why an Isaac Wunder order was granted in the first place.  

 Conclusions 

 194.              An Isaac Wunder order is one of the many inherent powers of the courts which can be employed, in exceptional circumstances, to prevent abuse of the judicial process. In light of the constitutional protection of the right of access to the courts, such orders are not an absolute bar to litigation, but operate as a filtering mechanism to restrain the repeated initiation of vexatious or unmeritorious proceedings. As the authorities make clear, an Isaac Wunder order will only be made where it is considered proportionate and necessary to do so, and the safeguard of a right of appeal will generally be available to the affected party. Such orders are not confined to the jurisdiction of the superior courts but may be made by the Circuit and District Courts in the exercise of their inherent powers to prevent an abuse of process in their courts within their jurisdiction. 

 195.              With regard to the specific context of family law proceedings, I find that there is nothing to prevent the making of an Isaac Wunder order in proceedings concerning child access, custody, or maintenance disputes. The best interests of a child is a relevant factor to consider before making such an order. As is demonstrated by the present appeal, however, a child's best interests may well be adversely affected by repetitious litigation and the consequent familial and financial strain caused by such proceedings. In this respect, I am satisfied that the Isaac Wunder order made by the Court of Appeal was neither disproportionate nor unduly restrictive, but rather a necessary response to a campaign of unmeritorious and oppressive litigation on the part of appellant on the basis of the evidence before the Court. 

 196.              Finally, it has been observed that, in addition to the power to issue an Isaac Wunder order, the courts have a range of powers at their disposal to safeguard the administration of justice when presented with a serial litigant or someone who disrupts or prolongs proceedings on a repeated basis as set out above. Where an application for leave to apply for judicial review is brought on a basis which is factually misleading, an application to set aside the grant of leave may be appropriate, as it was in the present case. Further, the availability of the DAR is an important safeguard to ensure the integrity of court proceedings where parties misrepresent what occurred in court on a previous occasion. These powers and procedures help to ensure that the twin objectives of protecting individual parties from serial or vexatious litigation and protecting the judicial process from excessive misuse of court time and resources, are realised. 

 197.              Accordingly, I would dismiss the appeal and affirm the order of the Court of Appeal.
